summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it, and that the view taken by the Orissa high Court was correct. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The concept of valuation date in terms of the last day of a period which is also the relevant period under the Income Tax Act, 1961, as the valuation date. [310F] (2) The scheme of the Wealth Tax Act shows that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last date of the previous year, as defined under the Act, as to what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets of an assessee under the Wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assessee are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lent investments could not he included in its net wealth of the asses see under the wealth Tax Act. [309F G] (3) The computation of the net wealth is correct and the conclusion was inescapable that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by the assessee. [311G H] Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth tax, ; , followed. (4) In the instant case, the computation of net wealth has been made by the Wealth ' Tax Officer on cashbasis basis interest on accrual of income on the valuation dates. The definition embodied in the substantive part of cl. (q) of section 2 indicates that broadly parliament has fixed on the lastday of the "previous year" as defined in the Income tax Act, and the figure of net assets of the assesses at the end of the 'previous year ' takes into account the financial activities of the appellant during that "previous years".

The respondent, a Time Keeper in the Department of preparing pay bills and other bills of work charg ing under the Punjab Government Servants (Conduct) Rules 1966, was appointed as Inquiry Officer. The Inquiry Officer framed charges against the respondent. In the inquiry report, the Inquiry Officer found that he had entered the name of Ashok Kumar in the pay roll for May 1969 and that he was a member of the staff of the Department. He also found him guilty of entering the name in the service register for May 1970 or that it was his duty to prepare the charge sheet. The respondent filed an appeal before the Central Administrative Tribunal, which dismissed the same on the ground that the punishment awarded to him was disproportionate to the delinquency of the respondent and was in stark contrast to the punishment imposed upon him. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent had entered into the name o f Ashok Kumar as his own brother and that there were others too, and as such he should not be allowed to take advantage of the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority on the basis of some of the findings of the Inquiry officer; (ii) the Tribunal was wrong in directing the Governor of Orissa to reconsider the penalty awarded to the respondent when the findings recorded as to h is misdemeanour were supported by legal evidence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has no power to interfere with the penalty on the grounds that it is not commensurate with the delinquence of the official. It is appropriate to rema nise the order of the Tribunal imposing a lesser penalty on a delinquent officer. [27C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent was not offered a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and accordingly the enquiry and consequential ord er of dismissal were found to be bad. The Tribunal had no power under section 27(1) of the Act to impose any punishment to meet the ends of justice. Where the person without enquiry is dis pute guilty, removed or reduced in rank solely on the view that he would have weighed with the authority in dismissing the public servant, the Tribunal has jurisdiction to exercise its power of review subject to the court permitting it. If the findings are perverse and the evidence is not such as to justify interference by the Tribunal, the Court has no juris diction to substitute its own judgment for that of the authority. [28D E] 1:3 The Tribunal imposed a lesser punishment on the respondent, but the High Court was in error in directing him to reconsider his penalty on ground that it would be justified by the rules. [29F G] 2.1 In the present case, there is no direct evidence of incapacity of the Court to review its own orders. It has not been shown that it had acted perversely or otherwise vitiated the ultimate conclusion or decision. The High Court has not interfered with the punishment if the conclusions are based on evidence even if some of it is found to have been irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [30G H] 2:2 In view of the principles to which we have call ed in the instant cases, the order imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot be sustained. [31B] 2 :3 The High Courts should not interfere with an order of punishment unless it is malafide is certain ly erroneous or perverse. [32C] 2?4 In the case of proceedings under article 226 of the Constitution, the High Courts have power to exercise their power of judicial review subject only to the Court permitting it to do so. If there has been an enquiry, the findings on all the Tribunal were not open to challenge in a writ petition under Article 32. [33D] 2(a) The Tribunal is not concerned with the competence or jurisdiction of the authorities to review their own orders and that the adequacy or sufficiency of penalty unless it was malafide is a matter exclusively within the jurisdiction of a compete ny authority. If, however, the finding of the enquiry officer or the Tribunal prima facie makes out a case of misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is difficult to say that the High court has power to substitute a penalty which in its opinion would be just a and proper in the circumstances of the case. [34F G; 35A B] 2.(b) The jurisdiction to impose penalty on an employee is conferred on the competent authority either by an Act of legislature or rules made under the provisions of the , or rules framed thereunder.

The appellants were the legal representatives of one of the deceased plaintiff. The suit was dismissed on the ground that he was not in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a decree for eviction could not be passed against him. The respondents filed an application under Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of possession on the grounds that the appellant was a lessee in respect of seven lots on an annual rent of Rs. 3600 payable in advance in three instalments; that he had paid the rent upto the end of December 1967 and that the first installment of 1968 but the owner, defendant No. 2, in collusion with defendant No 1 executed a deed of lease in favour of the latter effective from January 1, 1968 on the strength whereof defendant No 2 was in possession and that he has not been dispossessed; that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as constructive res judicata because the plaintiff was not a tenant or deemed tenant. The Trial Court upheld the plaintiffs contention and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the plaintiff had in fact been dispossessed, there was no question of granting an injunction and/or constructive resjudicata as found in Order 2 rule 2( 3) of C.P.C. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in holding that the second suit was not maintainable because the suit is barred by principle of res judicata. [1020B] 2.1 In a suit filed on the basis of a contract between the same parties and the cause of action for the former suit was different, it could be argued that the subsequent suit was one which was in respect to the land in question. The relief for possession was not claimed whereas in the second case the relief was for restoration or permanent injunction as contemplated under section 18(2) of Act. [1120C D] 2:2 In the instant case, the plaintiff came to court contending that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by section 9 of the Act, he was entitled to let out the property to defendant No1 and hence he was in lawful possession of it. The cause of actions for that suit was also not identical with the relief claimed in the earlier suit. [1220D E] 2 :3. In the present case, there is no question or specific relief which the plaintiff could have sought in the subsequent litigation. The real intention of the parties was to give rise to a situation where the remedy lies entirely under the Act and may have to be taken in the manner prescribed by or under the statute. [1320E] 2I2 In such a situation, the Civil Court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration/relief of possession to the deemed tenant.[1321G] 3:3.

The petitioners are employed as daily rated employees. They were paid minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They filed writ petitions in this Court challenging their claim. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitution and that it is open to the State to classify employees on the basis of qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Corporation has no regularly employed carpenters; that the petitioners are paid the minimum wages admissible to them under the Bonus Act and provident fund benefits under the Employees ' Provident Fund Act. Dismissing the writ petitions, HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay for Equal work is not a permissible exercise normally. It is open for the State Government to classify employ ees on the based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It cannot be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the peti tioners therefore fails and is rejected. [667B C] 2.1 The principle laid down in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) vs Union of India, ; at 245, is not applicable to the instant case because the petitioners were carpenter; better called as craftsmen. By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The two jobs by the merely ipse dixit of the volume or by the volume of work performed cannot be rated as equal. It was not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. The accuracy required by the job and the dexterity it entails may differ from job to job. It can be evaluated, by expert bodies. [668C D] 2:2 In the instant cases, the petitioners have been treated as construction workers and they are being paid the wages admissible under the Labour Act. They cannot enforce the right to "equal wages for equal Work". The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical proximity though owned by them unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the similar employer unless it was shown that the same sets of employees are comparable with the counterparts In other establishments. [669C D; 670A B] 2 :3 The petitioners are carpentants and better called " crafts men". By the General description of the work, one could come to their conclusion that each carpenter, one can come to them their rights elsewhere in accordance with law applicable to them.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, for murder of one Malan. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the accused alone for conspiracy under section 120A I. P.C., is unsustainable in law as at least two persons are required for an offence of conspiracy under Section 120A IPC and he relied upon a decision of this Court in Topandas vs State of Bombay, ; , which held that the appellant 's conviction and sentence awarded to him were not sustainable in law because at least 2 persons were required for the offence of criminal conspiracy under s.120A I P. C. and he had been rightly convicted and acquitted by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried along with accused 5 had been acquitted by a trial court of charge No. 1 framed under section 307 read with s. 120B IPC and accused 5 was not charged for the offences of murder of Malan, and acquitted accused 5 and directed him to be set at liberty forthwith and dismissed Criminal Appeal 38 of 1977 filed against that acquittal which was filed only against accused 2, 3, 4 and 7. [785C D] 2. The appellant had been convicted under section 201 read with Section 120B of I.p.C and sentenced for life imprisonment by the trial court. He had been wrongly convicted and convicted under s 302 readwith section 120 B I.Ps. and section 120(B I P C. [788E F] 3. In view of this technical flaw that the retracted judicial confessions of accused Nos. 5 and 6 were not reliable, the conviction and sentences awarded to them by the courts below are set aside and they are acquitted. [789G H] 4. The evidence of the approver P.W. 1 and the retracted confession of the co accused 5 is amply corroborated by other evidence and it acted also upon the retracted Judicial confession of appellant No. 5 in holding that the guilt of accused 6 for conspiracy u/s 120A read with S.120B I .P. C., could be sustained.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will executed by his father, filed a suit for possession of certain properties in dispute and a declaration that the said properties were his absolute property. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the will was not proved to be the last will and testament of the testator and that it was not genuine or valid and that the appellant had failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under the will. The High Court also held that even if it had been established that the testator had executed the will in favour of his father he was entitled to a life interest in items 1, 2 and 3 and decreed the appellant 's suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it could not be said that the execution of the Will was proved to have been executed by the testator. [447 D] (ii) The onus was on the propounder to prove the due and valid execution of a will propounded by him, such as the appellant himself, to prove his own title or its extinction by adverse possession respectively. It is true that if a caveat is filed alleging the exercise of undue influence, fraud or coercion in respect of the execution thereof, it would be necessary for the propounder, remove all clouds and to establish the sound and disposing state of mind and to prove them by cogent and satisfactory evidence. [427 D E] (iii) The burden was on him to prove affirmatively that the Will had been executed and attested by him. He has also failed to discharge this onus. It was not necessary for him to examine himself as a witness when he examined the attesting witnesses, to establish his due and proper execution of it. [545 D] In the present case, the High court had not fully discharged its duty under section 5 of the Indian Evidence Act. The evidence of the scribe and the appellant itself showed that the testatrix was in a sound and dispose of mind at the time when she signed the document. It would be difficult to treat her signature as an attesting witness on the instrument intending that the recitals and dispositions in the will should be her recitals and disposition. [444 D E; 445 A B] (iv) The evidence adduced by the appellant was not sufficient to prove her case about previous instruction of the testatrix and her signature on the document, which she had signed before her death, could not have been proved by cogent or satisfactory evidence, because, in recording these conclusions, the court had acted upon the evidence. It must be remembered that the High Courts were in error when they held that it had not properly considered all the relevant evidence and consequently the reasons given by them were open to serious challenge on the merits. [442 E F] (v) The appellant was entitled under section 3 of the Act to rely on the will, which is a very near relation of Kalbagal and even if she had no clear recollection as to what happened on the day when she attested the will her signature was not in accordance with law. [443 D E].

The appellant company was carrying on business of sale and sale of Arcotors, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by the appellant company. The goods were purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. Of course, it was very difficult to identify a taxable commodity merely by the use to which it may be put. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the common or ordinary use of the are carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast, through the projectors on cinema screens and sound recording and reproducing equipment lenses films and parts and accents in a particular area. It also found that the sales tax authorities were compelled to consider the use which is generally made of the arc carbins. The High Court held that these were not taxable under Entry 41 of the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562 E] 2. The definition of "accessory" is not exhaustive in which it occurs in a schedule in which description of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No. 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales tax Act, the words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No 11 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 12 for dictating, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon are belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that they are known as 'cinema are carbobons ' in the market. This finding was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the Andhra pradesh High Court that the goods under consideration are covered by the relevant entry No 4 of schedule 1 of Madras General sales Tax Act 1957. [562 H 564 A] 3. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that in both these cases what was decided was whether "welding electrodes" considered a connection with electricity, nor their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electrical goods". [563 B C] 4. The fact that the appellants can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage light and reproducing equipments lenses film films and part thereof is not sufficient to justify their view taken that the are Carbons under consideration here. [564 E F] 5. The words " parts thereof" in Entry 41, List II of the Seventh Schedule to describe the goods which might have been produced for useas an aid, or addition, a sense of a type writer so as to attract the tax under entry 18 of the second schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax, Act,1957. [563 E F].

The petitioners in these petitions are the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Rules. The petitioners in their writ petition challenged the validity of Rule 21 as it existed prior to the issue of the notification dated June 18, 1981 issued by the State Government under section 15 of the Act amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 with regard to the grant of royalty in respect of minor minerals. They also challenged the constitutional validity of rule 21 as being violative of Article 301 of the Constitution. The High Court struck down Rule 21 on the ground that it was discriminatory and violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 31(2). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and not for other purposes; (ii) Rule 21 which was substituted by the issue in 1981 was discriminatory in character. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy is made under a law made by the Central Government. It is not an imposition made by a law making authority on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applies. [412C] 2. Rule 21 of the Rules was enacted for purposes of regulation and development and conservation of minerals. It was not in the nature of fee which could be used only for specific purposes. Any tax realised by the Government from the lessees would not be violative of article 14 provided the classification is a reasonable one. [414D] 3. The State Government is entitled to grant concessions and exemptions wherever necessary having regard to purpose of the statute, the levy of royalty is incidental to the regulation and Development of minerals.[412E F] 4. Rule 33 A provides that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec ties covered by a mining lease are determined under section 3. Rule 18 of the rules provides that the competent officer may notify areas of limestone, Black Trap, sand stone and building stones for the purpose of grant of quarrying parawana, as he deems fit. When any area is so notified no quarry leases shall be given for such notified area. Rule 23 A provides for the levy and covered by the Rules which says that no royalty shall be payable for an Area exceeding 10 per cent of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty is payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year. The rule also provides that any person who manufactures or manufac tured stone or sand mining leases in respect thereof to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [413D E] 5. Rule 22 which was inserted by the Gujarat Amendment Rules, 1966 is discriminatory in nature.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village in the District of Nagapattinam. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge and restored the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession is "regulated by usage" and therefore the office of a hereditary trustee is in the nature of property. HELD: (i) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [426 B] (ii)The expression "regulated" in section 6(9) must be construed along with the phrase "sucession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. The word 'successor ' in relation,to property and right means the trustee of a religious institution. [425 C D] (iii)The words "regulatedby usage" in s 6(1)(c) must mean their normal rules of inheritance under the Indian law are modification of Hindu Law by usage. In the present case, there is no warrant for this argument. The phrase "regulated ' in section six(9), does not mean a hereditary trust or the office to which he has been appointed. [427 D E] (iv)The word " succession ' in the context of section 6 (9) means that on the death of an existing mahant if he left any, and failing disciples, any one of his spiritual kindred. Such a succession is described as not hereditary in the sense that on condition that the scheme of such succession is still in force. [527 D E; 428 A] (v)The term "suecession" is identical in both the Acts. The definition includes three types of cases: (1) succession to the office and (2) succession being specifically provided for by the founder. The artificial definition of hereditary trustee in section 2(9)(c), therefore, includes even such cases. But the election to the post of trustee in the present ease is for a fixed period of one year and not for life.

The prosecution case against the appellant was that he along with two others, armed with a knife and a knife, had killed one of them. The deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). He got up and saw the accused hitting him with knife. He got down and saw two persons running ahead of him. He ran to his elder brother who was sleeping near him. When he went near him, he was already dead. The appellant was declared absconder. On hearing a noise, the deceased came out and saw one person lying on the ground with knife and another with knife, and that he had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and witnessed the incident. He also saw two other persons running towards the place where the deceased was sitting. The younger brother of the deceased who was a lepered brother was running after stabbing him with a dagger. He was also seen by the deceased when he went to the scene of occurrence. The doctor who conducted the postmortem examination found nine injuries on the body of the dead body and one of the incised wounds, on the left side of the neck, left arm, on right side of chest, on both sides. On the other hand, the High Court acquitted the second accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court had not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4 and that the conviction and sentence were bad. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered various broad facts which should definitely weigh with the court while appreciating oral testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence, but the fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased had been only mentioning the name of accusedkali was also immaterial. [710E F] 2. The evidence of the sole eye witness is true that the appellant attacked the deceased with knife on his chest and stabbed him with an dagger. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may also not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that there is no evidence to show that the other assailants who arrived at the place a little earlier than PW 4 did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. It also stands to reason that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4, who arrived in the place, a little later, for information with regard to the assailants.

The assessee was a partner in a firm of solicitors. The firm was carried on by the firm as its managing agents and the realisations were to be divided amongst the partners. The business was carried out by the firms. The assessee was carrying on the business of carrying on business in the names of Amarchand and Amarchand. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amounts received after the death of Amar Chand were not liable to income tax as they were not income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations of the assets of Amarachand. The Tribunal, however, held that though for different reasons the amounts which were received by the heirs and legal representatives of Amarichand were not taxable, the amount was assessable under section 24B of the Income tax Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the amounts in question were not exempt from income tax in view of the provisions of section 24 B of the Act; (2) the amount which were sought to be taxed and which had been held not to be liable to tax as received by Amarchand, and (3) the assessee was entitled to claim that the said amounts were not assessable to income Tax. HELD : (i) The amounts which are sought to have been taxed and who are not liable for payment of income tax are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable under section 23B of Income tax. [707 B] (ii) The provisions of s 24B do not extend to tax liability of the estate of a deceased person beyond the previous or the account year in which that person dies. In the present case the amounts were sought by the legal representatives to be assessed to income taxes under section 25B as their income had been received by them before his death and they were therefore liable for the payment of tax just as the deceased would have been liable when the income was received by him and he survived. [607 C D] (iii) The amount which are claimed to have become due to the heirs of Amar Chandra and are not exempt under section 26B of Act. [700 E F] (iv) The liability for the income received in this year is not a charge in respect of the income of a person after his death. [650 C D].

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They challenged the Act as ultra vires the Constitution on the ground that article 16(3) of the Constitution was violated by the provisions of article 16 (b). The High Court held that article 3(1) did not apply to the case and quashed the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the power conferred by section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957, was a valid law prescribing the requirement as to residence in a particular part of the State and that the provisions were ultra vires. HELD : The contention must be negatived. Article 16(b) does not require any discrimination among other things on the grounds of residence. Realising this that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have been to be prevented and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to he prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made applicable to the State of Andhra Pradesh. [121 E F] The words "residence within the State" in article 16 are controlled by the words 'residence ' or its duration rather than its location within the state. The word 'State ' here is not controlled by any other name but it must be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. [122 G H] In the present case, the petitioners were employed between December 26, 1956, and July 1, 1968, and therefore, they could not claim to be a citizen under article 16 of the . [123 B C] The contention that Parliament had no discrimination among others on the basis of residence within the meaning of article 35(b), was not correct. The words 'any requirement ' cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. These words bear upon the kind of residence or its strength rather than their location within tho State. [123 E F]. The contention of the petitioners, that Parliament has no discrimination, among other matters, on the allegation of residence is not correct and must be rejected. [124 C] In view of the decision in State of Bombay vs M/s. A. V. R. Tendolkar ; , the contention that the Mulki Rules existing in the former Hyderabad State must continue to operate by virtue of article 5(b).

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them also for offences punishable under sections 467 and 471 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of section 103 of the Evidence Act, (2) the seizure of the articles was not vitiated by any irregularity or illegality; (3) the conviction having been based on circumstantial evidence the High court had no jurisdiction to set aside the acquittal and convict him in respect of offences under sections 466 and 471. HELD : (i) The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission by post. [415 D] (ii)The mere fact of possession does not suffice to show that the articles were delivered to the addressees. The presumption under section 103 is that the goods are delivered to them. It has not been found that they have been secreted by the appellant. Therefore, the conviction cannot be sustained. [416 G H] (iii)The search was in the exclusive possession of the appellant and there was no evidence that it was ever with him. The mere circumstance that there was even a lapse of several years in delivering the postal article did not suffice for holding that he had secreting the articles. [414 C D] In the present case, the search of the house in which the appellant lives along with his father and of which the key was furnished by the father was merely an incriminating circumstance to incriminate the son. The search was therefore illegal inasmuch it was not established that the almirah was in any way connected with the appellant or that he was in their exclusive possession. [413 D E] (iv)The absence of a search was no ground for holding the appellant guilty of an offence under section 53 of the Act.

The appellant, a public servant, filed a complaint before the Nyaya Panchayat alleging that he had been abused and assaulted by the respondent. The Magistrate ordered investigation of the case and submitted a report to the High Court. The High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings before the magistrate. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court was not justified in interfering with the order of the Single Judge. The mere fact that the Magistrate wanted to avoid the petitioner 's affidavit being brought on record by declaring him guilty would not be sufficient to give him an opportunity to accept the mere statement of the party that the High court had stayed proceedings before it. (ii) In such matters those who assert that a person had knowledge of the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If there is any doubt, the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of Court. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of contempt of court for disobeying the order. The question then arises whether the Sarpanch and the Pan chas had knowledge about the existence of the orders of the High Courts dated December 20, 1963. The only material before them was the application dated December 25, 1963 which was not supported by any affidavit sworn to before a person authorised to administer oaths. [121H 122A] (iii) In the circumstances of this case, there is no force in the contention that the Sarpanch had knowledge that a particular person had know of the existence or the High Commissioner 's order. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M about the filing of the application before him. At any rate he has apparently no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before him when no proceeding is pending before him, and it is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of the court for disobedience of its order unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge or information about the order passed by the High Panchayat. [122B C] Hoshiar Singh vs Gurbachan Singh ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302, I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge, Etawah, for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the entire report dictated by him was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the entire investigation made by the police was inadmissible under section 162, Cr. P.C.; (ii) the extra judicial confession was not admissible in evidence and (iii) the appellant had been rightly convicted of murder. HELD: (i)(a) The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. [206 B] (b) The evidence of the appellant was corroborated by the evidence of P.W. 2, who stated that he had purchased a sword a day before the incident and deposited it with him at the police station after he had dictated the report. Both the courts below have found that the appellant 's confession was voluntary and true. [207 C] (c) The High court erred in rejecting the statement of the approver on the basis of the extrajudicial confession made by him to the Police Officer. It is not a matter of surprise that he wakes up and proceeds to the spot from where the splashing sound which is supposed to be due to the wading of the neel gais, came. [208 E] (d) The appellant had no motive for committing the murder. He had been falsely implicated in the case. He was rightly convicted under section 307 I. P., C. and sentenced him to death by the trial court. [209 G H] (e) The confession of a co accused is admissible in terms of section 162 Cr.P C. [210 B] In the instant case, the extra Judicial confessions were not ordinarily considered with respect to the appellant. The evidence was corroborated in material particulars and the conviction could not be upheld. [211 D E] The High Courts erred in holding that the confession was made by a person 's own brother 's house and that it was not proved that he was a co convicter of the crime.

The respondent No. 1, a local authority, filed an election petition challenging the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 (No. 23 of 1956). The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the respondent No 1 was not prompt in moving the High Court and that the petitioner did not have any objection to the inclusion of his name in the electoral rolls on October 19, 1978. On appeal by special leave, the High court held that respondent No 2 had asked for a further direction to be issued to the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31, 1978, and directed the issue of notice of the petition and stay application to the Respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the Rules. The High Court also held that the writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Courts as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the period of 20 days had been fixed for entertaining claims and objections, a large number or people who could have filed claims and objection were prevented from preferring them within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule 3(1), the High Commission had no jurisdiction to do so. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The power of the High 'Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High, finding that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue has been brought to its notice by the petitioners immediately after it was noticed by them. [497G H] 2. The order of the Court is set aside and the matter remitted back to the High for a fresh decision on merits. [498A B] 3. The writ petition filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 5 was rightly rejected by the Single Judge as there were no satisfactory explanations for the inordinate delayed filing of it till December 28, 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the notices issued under rule 4(i) of Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication) Rules, 1963.

The appellant was the director of a company and its directors were prosecuted for failure to comply with the provisions of section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913. The High Court held that if no general body meeting had been held and the balance sheet and profit and loss account had not been laid before a general body, there could be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 132 and that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 134(4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the principle accepted by this Court in Park vs Lawton, ; , that a company or its directors in a prosecution under section 32 and section 133 of the 1913 Act could not in defence to such prosecution rely upon their own failure to call the general body meetings as a defence to the prosecution; (2) the principles laid down in Park 's case were not applicable to the present case, and (3) the appellant had been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 of 1956. HELD : (i) The High Courts have taken a similar view and have held that the principle is consistent with the principle embodied in Park v Lawton; , and (ii) the provisions unmistakably indicate, as they are clearly clear, that the holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balance sheets and profit & loss account was a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. If no general Body meeting is held, the persons concerned cannot be said to have committed a default in complying with those provisions. [415 D E] (iii) The appellant had not taken any objection to call a general meeting as a prosecution witness and that there was no failure to calling a general election meeting. [416 G H] (iv) The principle accepted in Park V Lawton 's Case is that the requirement of section 134 of the Act is that this section should be interpreted in the light of the law made by Parliament and not on the necessity of their being laid before the general meeting of the company not being fulfilled. [414 C D] (v) The provisions unmistakably indicated, as it was, that if the balance Sheet is not adopted at the general meetings before which it is laid, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance Sheets and the profit and Loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, would be made punishable under sub section (4) of that section. [413 D E; 414 A B] (vi) The provision in Park was not consistent with section 132 of the 1956 Act and therefore the requirement that copies of such documents should be filed before the company at the General meeting was not complied with. [411 C] (vii) The presumption under section 133 is rebuttable and there can be no doubt that the presumption under the section is for default in compliance with the provision. But it is possible to conceive of the Law providing that the balance of accounts so laid before it should be kept open for the company to do so even though the default may be wilful. [409 E] The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors., ; , referred to. (viii) The contention that the provisions in sections 134 and 136 of the Indian Companies Act are not complied, is without substance. The section lays down various requirements which are to be complied with by the company under its first four sub clauses and sub cl. (5) is the penal sub section which penalises failure to do any act in complying therewith. [420 G H; 420 A] (ix) The penalty under these sections is for non compliance with section 134 and not for failure of the Director to call for a general notice as required by section 132.

The respondent was charged with offences under sections 3 and 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, which was replaced by the West Benabari Act, 1950. The trial commenced on August 9, 1951, and the accused were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment by the Special Court. On appeal the High Court held that section 5(1) of the Act had no application to the case as it did not provide for a speedier trial but only provided for the trial by a special court and did not make any distinction between offences under section 3 and those under section 5. The State appealed to this Court with certificate. Held, that the classification made in section 5 (1) was valid and the classification must be held to be reasonable. The classification must not be arbitrary but must be based on some qualities or characteristics which are peculiar to persons or who are left out but those qualities or attributes must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The distinction between the two classes of offences is, therefore, well established and that in each case judges must look straight into the heart of things and regard the facts of each case concretely much as a jury would do; and yet not quite as a result of the enactment of the law itself. The fact that the State can under section 269(1), make a provision for the speedior trial of certain offences does not necessarily mean that judges are to deter mine what is for the good of the people and substitute their individual and personal opinion for that of the Government of the day or that they may usurp the functions of the legislature. The provisions for the provi sions of section 5 of Act No. 1 of 1949, in so far as it empowers the State Government to direct a special Court to try such offences or classes of cases or classes thereof or classes or classes Of cases or class of cases, or classes, of cases and classes of case, or class or classes for classes of Cases or classes and classes or cases of cases of a kind fraught with the most serious consequences to the individuals concerned, for special and adequate reasons having a relation to their object. The scheme of the impugned Act is that it provides for the procedure to be followed in such cases by a Special Court and does not provide any machinery for the speedy trial of such offences.

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He was later promoted to the post of Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in the Medical College. The post of Professor of radiology in the medical college was a post belonging to the Central Health Service and continued to work in that capacity till October 8, 1964. By an order dated January 1, 1965, the Government of India, Ministry of Health, Health & Family Planning Department of Health by its letter dated April 6, 1965 directed that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the said post as he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality. The appellant was not only holding the post as an Associate Professor but also performing the duties attached to the teaching post of Radiologist. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated April6, 1965 and the order of the Central Government dated January 17, 1976. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the post was divided into two classes viz., Class I and Class II and the appellant was also performing his duties as an Assistant Professor of Pathology in a medical college and treated as an assistant Professor of P Associate Professor in that Department. It was further submitted that the teaching experience gained by him while holding the said posts was different and the post could not he taken into consideration for determining his eligibility for appointment as Associate Professor. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant could be considered to have been appointed to the Post of Associate professor in Ma reciprocology in Malulana Azad medical College, which had fallen vacant in 1973. As a necessary consequence, it was eligible to be considered by the Union Public Service Commission for appointment of Assistant Professor as Associate Professors of Radiological Institute in Mahammed Azad Medical college. [8E F] 1.2 The Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, New South Wales, has been using the Central Excise and Taxation Commissioner 's Office Manuals for the purpose of interpreting the expression "engineering of personnel" in the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956. The said Rules are intended to give effect to the object of the Act. [88G H] 1:3. It is not for the Court to give the appellant promotion or make his appointment to a post of Assistant Director of Radiology. [89A B] 2.1 In the instant case, the Central Govern ment has been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Maulana Nehru Medical College for the Mulana Azad College, the appellant is not holding the posts of an Associate professor of Radiologists (ex officio) in the Irwin Hospital since October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into account. [90G H; 91A] 2:2. The Ministry has been utilising his services to the appellant as Associate Dean of Radiography (exoth erly) in Mahammad Azad Medical Colleges for the purposes of teaching the five years of super officio in the Morman Hospital since the post is not belonging to an Associate Professors or Assistant Professor in a speciality hospital having at least six years ' service experience out of 12 years standing in the Grade through the Union Government. The mere designation of the appellant does not give him a right to hold the post. [91B C] 2 :3. The fact that he was holding the teaching posts in a teaching hospital like the Irin Azad Medical Institute, which is a teaching post, cannot prevail. [92C D] 2(a) It is for the Union of India to advertise the post and appoint an Assistant Professors of radiotherapist Grade II. The only designation of such a post does not confer him a vested right on the post or that he can always apply irrespective of the fact whether or not he is in the line of promotion.

The appellant company had taken on lease a piece of land for the purpose of manufacturing tea. The workmen were paid minimum wages and this was covered by item 2 of the Schedule attached to the Order of reference. The Company made an application under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was no identical industry in the region comparable with the company and therefore, the workmen were entitled to bonus on any further rise in price index. On appeal by the workmen it was contended before this Court that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in not making calculation of surplus available on the basis of the Full Bench Formula approved by this Court in French Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs The Workmen, ; , and that the principle laid down by this court in French Motors (India) Ltd. case was applicable to the present case. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had not committed any error of fact or law requiring interference by this tribunal. [674 E] In the instant case, the Tribunal committed an apparent error of record in arriving at its decision and consequently the total minimum wage packet of a workman in the company should be fixed at Rs. 95. This was done on the assumption that the minimum wage fixed by the tribunal was not uniform throughout the period of five years. [678 F] (ii) The finding of fact recorded by the Industrial Tribunal is based on an erroneous approach and cannot be sustained. It is well settled that in appropriate cases, of making a direction linking the dearness allowance element of a wage to the Price Index, it should be made clear that such linking may be permissible by holding that the workmen are providing any such amenities which are different from those being provided by those concerns in the Region which are being charged with the price index and that there is no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average minimum wage payable to the workmen. [677 G H] In re: French Motor car Co., ; , referred to. (iii) The principle laid out by this Courts in French Transport Car Co., Ltd. Case, was not applicable to industrial disputes and the Tribunal was right in holding that there could be no justification to introduce a new element of payment of bonus to casual and badIi workers at this stage. [676 G H; 677 A] (iv) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed, as that year was still running when the award was given by the Tribu nal on the 11th January, 1964.

The appellant, a partnership firm, had been assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, assessed the appellant 's income under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The appellant challenged the validity of that notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notices issued by the Income tax officer. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The report submitted by the Incometax Officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner were not produced. [448 D] (ii) The appellant could not have issued a notice under section 149 of the Income Tax Act. Under section 151 of the , it is incumbent upon the Income. tax Officer to have issued notice under that section, as of right, to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year to tax on income or loss or depreciation allowance originally assessed/allowed. He has not even come to a prima facie conclusion that the transactions to which he referred are not genuine transactions. He is not satisfied that this was a fit case for issue of a notice. [449 E F] (iii) The Commissioner had mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that the transaction to which the appellant referred were not genuine. He appeared to have recorded that he had been satisfied that these persons were the names lenders and the transactions were bogus. He had not even came to a Prima facie conclusion, that the dealings to which him referred are of taking loans from various parties of Calcutta. From D.I.s Invitely accorded permission, he did not itself record that the appellant was satisfied with the facts mentioned in his report. [450 G H] (iv) The order of Commissioner was based on a report submitted under section 151 (2). The report was not produced and therefore could not be relied upon. [451 B C] (v) The assessment made by the income tax Officer must have been a fit one for the issue of notice under s 148. [452 E F]. (vi) The failure to mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit cases for the issuance of a show cause notice under S.148, does not fulfil the requirements Of section 151.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in the manufacture of textiles and other goods, was started in 1902 and its business was carried on by two independent partnerships. The partners constituted a new firm which had been reconstituted by an agreement dated December 6, 1918. The firm was dissolved by an order of the Ruler of the erstwhile State of Bombay under which it was reconstituted. The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of certain sums of money from the respondent firm on the ground that the business in question was carried out by a firm which was dissolved and its businesses were split up into two and carried on with effect from November 13, 1947, and the partnership deed was registered on February 7, 1948. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the business of the firm was carried in a new name and the business was not discontinued on April 1, 1939, and (2) even if it was held that on May 30, 1939 there was a discontinuance of the original business, the family could be said to have ceased to exist and the income, profits and gains of the period between April 13, 1938 and March 28, 1939 were liable to tax under the Act of 1918. HELD: (1)(a) The business in which the appellant had been subjected to tax was not a dissolution of the partnership but was dissolved on November 6, 1947. [287 D] (b) The firm being a new one, it could not be said that there was succession by another person for the purpose of section 26 or for the purposes of section 25 (4). [286 E F] (c) The fact that the partner was not taken on in the original partnership deed did not make him a partner. It was only if there was discontinuance of his business before 1948 or a succession not amounting to a mere change in the constitution of the family, that the appellants could be denied the benefit of section25(4). But even assuming that the firm had ceased to be a dissolved firm, it would not disentitle the appellant from claiming relief under sub section (4) only in respect of the money lending business. [286 G H] (2)(a). The fact of the partners constituting the firm did not affect the question of relief under s 25(3) because the partnership was dissolved in 1947 and the family was entitled to the benefit thereof, continued uninterruptedly till 1948 or for a period of three years. [288 B C] (3) The appellant could not claim the benefit under section 26(4), because, as the partner had been allotted to the father and the rest to the son, he was not in fact taken on the original firm 's name. [289 E F]. (b)(i) The partnership deed dated December 7, 1918 was a registered one and the appellant could be assessed under the Indian Income tax Acts of 1918 and 1949 only if it had been dissolved by a change in its constitution. [290 G] (ii) The mere change of ownership did not count and sections 25(1) and 26(2) do not apply at the same time. The business of a firm was not even in contemplation of section 23(2).

The respondent, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses. The appellant 's case was that the suit properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband and his two sons. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties belonged exclusively to the respondent and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th undivided share. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit property belonged to joint family; (2) the respondent had effected partition of the suit house between himself and his brothers; (3) the appellant 'S 's 1/24 share in the joint Hindu Family properties was only 1/25th, that the respondent 's father had effected a partition of that house by metes and bounds during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s interest upon his death; (4) the plaintiff 's share in her own property was only one half and that therefore, by reason of the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, the pre conditions of section six were satisfied. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The suit properties belong to joint Hindu family and are self acquisitions. [766D] (b) The respondent 'S had effected the partition of his coparcenary property by metes & bounds during his life time between him and his sons. [764B C] (c) The appellant had a share in a joint family property, the fourth being, Khandappa 's wife 's husband '. The proviso to section 6 states that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. [774C D] (d) The proviso does not provide further that in calculating the quantum of share of the heirs, the court may take into account the share of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property at the time of his death. [754D E] (e) The Explanation to section six states that where a male died after the commencement of the Act, she would have a 1/4th share therein and two or four annas share each. [765F G] (f) The expression "the widow ' shall be deemed to be" the share in property that would have been allotted to him if a partition had taken place immediately before his death". One must therefore imagine a state of affairs in which a little prior to Khandappa, a partition may take place between him & his two brothers. [664G H] (g) The explanation to section6 does not mean that the share should be ascertained on the basis that they bad separated from one another and had received a share therein during the life time of the deceased. [678A B] (2)(a) In the instant case, the widow 's claim was based on the provisions contained in section 6 which provides for the determination of the shares of the widow and then to ignore it for calculating the amount of the share. The High Court has rightly held that the widow had a 1 /4th interest in the coparcenary property and the appellant had 5/24 half share in it. [688B C; F] (3)(a). The proviso thereto will further the legislative intent in regard to the enlargement of the right of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener to property as also the right to demand partition like any male member of the family. [691C D]. (b). The High court was not justified in limiting the plaintiff to obtain a share equal to that of a son. [702D] Shiramabai Bhimgonda vs Kalgonda, A.I.R. 1975 Orissa 194; Shiram Bai Bhimgondi vs Kagonda, I.L.R., ; and Durgah Ram vs Gangadhar, A,I. R. 1974 Orissa 194, referred to. (c). The view which the High court has taken is correct.

The appellant Corporation, a public sector undertaking, was constituted under the Life Insurance Corporation of India Act, 1956. The Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1960, came to be promulgated by the Central Government on January 19, 1956, providing for the vesting of the management of the life insurance business in the State of Kerala. Section 11(2) of the said ordinance provided that every whole time employee of an insurer whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it shall retire on completion of 58 years of age or at any time thereafter if his efficiency was found to have been impaired. The appellant Corporation was required to retire on completing 58 years from the date of retirement on or after 1st September, 1956 but before that date the Corporation decided to nationalise the life of its employees. In exercise of the power conferred by section 11(1) of Act, the management took over the management and appointed the appellant as an employee of the Corporation on or about May 31, 1956 and provided for its management. The respondent Corporation was directed to retire from service on June 30, 1986. On the passing of the ordinance, the appellant Corporation decided that the age of retirement in his case could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post. The Corporation accordingly issued an order dated September 3, 1956 under section 11 (2) read with section 49(2), directing the appellant corporation to retire the respondent on completion Of 58 years. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of retirement and the consequential orders passed by the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the employees of the respondent Corporation belonging to Class I and Class II were not entitled to continue in service beyond 58 years, and that the appellant was estopped from claiming the benefit of the impugned order of compulsory retirement. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the age Of retirement had been fixed at 55 years, the retirement age was a valid classification and Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution had not been violated. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The regulations and other provisions as in force immediately before the commencement of the Life insurance Corporation (Amendment) Act, 1981, with respect to the terms and conditions of service of employees and agents of the corporation including those who became employees and agent of the Corpo ration on or before 1st Septem ber 1956 were not applicable to the respondent corporation. [204C] 2. The Regulations and other relevant provisions as contained in the Act are as follows: (a) The age of superannuation of employees shall be 60 years, subject to the condition that they shall retire at the age provided for by the regulations. (b) The employees belonging to class I or Class II who were appointed after 1 st September 1956 but prior to 1st October 1956 were required to superannuate on completionof 58 years in accordance with the provisions of section 11 of the Act, and (c) The retirement age of the employees shall retire from the Corporation before they attained the age prescribed by the Regulations. [205D E] 3. The regulation and other provision as in the present case are not violative of Article 14 and16 of the Constitu tion. [206E F] 4. The Regulation and other Provisions as in existence immediately before commencement of Life Insurance Act, 1961, have not been implemented so far as the age is concerned. [207F G] 5. The employees of Class I or class II who had entered service of the Corpora tion after 1.9. 1956 were governed by the Life Assurance Corporation (Staff) Regulations, 1960 and the regulations made thereunder. [208G] 6. The provisions in the Provident Fund Act and the Rules are not violated. [209H; 210A] 7. The age Of superannuation of the employee is fixed at 58 years which varies from year to year. It is only in 1965 that the Corporation has been created by the Act. In 1973, the age was increased to 55 years. [211C D] 8. The retirement of the existing employees in Class I & Class II and Class III categories are governed by different conditions of serv ice. The new sub section (2), (3) and (4) of section 49 of the Employees ' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 have been given retrospective effect from 20th June, 1979. [212D] 9.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India stating that the Judge had been given an impression that he was not a Judge but a politician who had come to Barwani in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court. The letter stated that the Judges of the Bar Association were very poor and that they had failed miserably in all fields. The appellants took a copy of their letter to this Chief Minister, who was present at the hearing. They also wrote a note stating that if in view of this Hon 'ble Court the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by them and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the letter did not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The letter in the instant case was addressed by the deponent to the Governor of Punjab with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon ' blemis sion of a Judge or this Court should steer clear of all avoidable controversial matters. [245E] 1.2 In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communication in question was brought personally by two members of the bar association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a open cover addressed by one of the members of Bar Association, Bhiwni to Chandigarh. The deponent further stated that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Honble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. [246G H] 1:3. The contents of the letter were not disputed and challenged. It was intended to be a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. In order that the action may be taken for any reasons contempt of Court, one would he more swer than the affidavit himself. Therefore, the deponent tender his apology to this Hon`ble Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance. [243A B] 1 :4. The matter did not constitute any contempt. The contempt proceedings were dropped.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture of textile and other articles. The company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded payment of tax. The Income tax Officer, after investigation, found that the appellant had committed an offence under section 5(1) of the Act, and issued a notice to the appellant under section 6(5) Of the Act asking him to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure 'B ' to the report of the Commission. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Tribunal held that the provisions of sections 5(2), 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Indian Income tax Act were not applicable to the case and that section 5 (1) Of section 5 Of the said Act was ultra vires the Central Government. The High Court, on a reference under article 226, held that section 6 of the said Indian Income Tax Act did not apply to the present case as it had been made in accordance with the provisions contained in section 34 of the , and that the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act was a good substitute for that prescribed by section 7 Of the Indian Incometax Act. Held, that the proceedings taken under section 3(4) Of Act XXXVII of 1947 were not covered by section 5 of the Central Act. The procedure prescribed under the Act in so far as affects the persons proceeded against under that sub section being a piece of discriminatory legislation offends against the provisions Of article 14 of the Constitution and is thus void and unenforceable. Held further, that section 7 of the impugned Indian Income. tax Act did apply to all persons who had similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they were persons who have not truly disclosed their income and had evaded payment thereof. The provisions of section 5 are in pari materia with those of section 6 Of the Central Provinces and Berar Companies Act and the procedure for reference under section 23(3) of that Act is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure provided by the Indian Act. Consequently, the proceedings against the appellant were not barred by article 14 Of the Constitution. Held also, further, the provisions in sections 5 (4), 5 (5) and 5 (6) of Act XXXVIII of 1947 are valid and unenforceable and unenforceable under articles 14 and 19 of the constitution.

The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business as a commercial establishment. The primary objects of the Federation were to promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade, transport, industry and manufacture, finance and all other economic subjects and to encourage or facilitate the export of goods, industrial undertakings and manufacturers. The appellant, an association of companies, was registered under section 26 of the , with its registered office at New Delhi. The Federation had a branch office in New Delhi and New Delhi etc. The establishment was not a commercial establishments within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The Association was registered as a Commercial Establishment under section 2 (9) of that Act. In the year 1963, the appellant company filed an application for prosecution of its Secretary, the Federation, under the . The Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishments, Delhi, called upon the Federation to register its establishment and submit its report. On February 4, 1964, the Association made a complaint under the , against the Federation and its employees alleging that it had been carrying on a profession as it was "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". The Federation filed a complaint before the Chief Inspector who held that the appellant was not an "establishment" within the definition of " commercial establishment" in section 2 of the . He, therefore, issued process for the prosecution of the Secretary. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activity of the Association carried on in the premises was a business or trade and that the writ petition was maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the activities of the respondent were not a " commercial" establishment within the expression "commercial establishment" as defined in section2(5), and (ii) the activity amounted to a 'business ' within the term of the definition, and therefore, the High Court was wrong in holding that it was not 'industry '. HELD: (i)(a) The definition of commercial establishment includes, inter alia, "commercial establishments" and "industrial establishments". [356D] (b) The activities of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the purview if the activity carried on by it amounts to a busi ness. Therefore, the commercial or industrial entertainments were also considered as an 'establishment ' within section 2.(5) and the definition was applicable in the case of a place in order to fall within the purview of the expression 'commercial establishment '. [356F] (c) The activity of a Registered Society, charitable, or other Trust will not taken it out from the definition if the activities carried on are by it amount to a business. [337B C] (d) The word "business" in Section 2(4) of Act is wide enough to include 'shop ' and ' commercial establishment ' in section 25. [359D] In the instant case, the respondent was a company within the scope of the term "commercial Establishment". It was not engaged in any activity of any individual traders or businessmen. The respondent was an association which was a "public" establishment under the Act and therefore the activities were connected with trade and business, generally. [360E] (e) The mere fact that the respondent is a company does not mean something by which a profit is made. But putting aside the question whether they carry on a business would be a commercial activity or not. [361F G] (f) The High court was right in holding the activities amounted to "business". [362G H] (g) The respondent is an association, which is a "commercial" within section2 (5) Of the Act, and the appellant is not engaged any "establishment". [361H; 362A] (2) The expression " commercial Establishment" in s.2(4), includes a 'shops ' and a commercial Establishment '. A place in the order of the association is not in the nature of a " Commercial establishment", but it should be premises where, (a) the businessmen or traders or trademen or trade establishments are carried on, or (b). The fact remains that it carries on systematic activities not only to assist its members but also other traders or businesses.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his successors. The income tax authorities assessed the assessee to agricultural income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the amount received by him as an allowance during the previous year of assessment was revenue income liable to tax under section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the income tax was not agricultural income as defined in section 2(1)(a) of Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the allowance in question was revenue receipt and not taxable; and (ii) the source of the income was clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it was not agriculture income as contemplated by section 4 (3)(vii). HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the allowance was revenue. [707 D] The word 'derived ' is not a term of art but a term which is used in the definition itself.
