In the present case, the source and character of the assessee are altered when a part of the Income tax is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration. Both the source as well as the character of income appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the nature of the receipt, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. [077 D] Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Wesleyan and General Assurance Society, , referred to. The High Courts were right in treating the allowance as revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. [087 E F] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, ; and Commissioner of Income tax Bihar & Orissa vs Raja Bahadur Kamakhaya Narayan Singh and Ors., , referred. Per Hidayatullah, J. The allowance is revenue income. The appellant was entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 3(3) (viii). [078 G] The High court was right that the allowances were in fact a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the assesses 's predecessor in interest.

The respondents in C.A. No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors Grade A on various dates in pursuance of a circular dated 6th November, 1962 issued by the Ministry of Defence, which provided that the Diploma holders who had been appointed as Supervisor 'A ' and in equivalent grades should be treated as having been promoted to Chargeman II. The appellants in CAs Nos. 441 and 442 of 1981 filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the said circular dated 4th April, 1983 and the judgment of this Court dated 2nd February, 1981. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the direction given by this Court on 2nd Febru ary, 1981 was not applicable to the case of the appellants as they had been promoted in pursuance thereof and that the respondents were entitled to be treated at par with the other similarly situated persons. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the said Circular dated 6 th November,1962 was not a direct recruit ment Grade 'A but only such a Supervisor Grade 'B ' who immediately before the coming into force of the order dated 28th December, 1965 and the circular dated 20th January, 1966 stood in a class separate from those whose promotion were to be made thereafter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondents in Civil Appeal No. 442 of1981 are on the same footing as they have been promoted before that date. [106G] 2.1 It is not a fit case for initiating any proceedings for contempt again st the respondents. [107A B] 2(i) The appellants cannot be granted the same relief which was granted to them in Civil Appeals No.441 of 1981. [108C D] 2.(ii) The High Courts have failed to exercise their jurisdiction for contempt against the respondents and hence they are not entitled to initiate proceedings for Contempt again stances again st them. [109E F] 2 (iii) It is well settled that a writ petition cannot be entertained by a Court in respect of an order passed by it. A writ petition is not maintainable in respect thereof simply on the basis of the judgment in Civil appeal No. 440 of 1981, which indicates that but for the decision in Civil appeals No. 439 of 1981 the High Courts would constitute the basis for the exercise of jurisdiction. [110F G] 2:2 It is also well settled by this court that it is not necessary to issue a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to implement the order of this court dated 2 nd February,1981 only on paper inasmuch as they are Supervisors 'A and 'B`. The said order has been passed in exercise of the power conferred under Rule 8 of Order 1 of 1962. [111D E] 3. It is clear from the judgment that the High courts have not exercised any jurisdiction for initiating proceedings for willful disobedience again stantial, non compliance with Article 16. [112F G].

The appellant State Transport Authority, by its order dated February 1, 1984 granted three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation. The first respondent was a stage carriage operator and the second respondent was the permit holder. The second respondent had to be denied the grant of permits since he had not got a certificate of approval from the Central Government. The appellant State Road Transport Corporation filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the grant. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that having regard to rule of preference envisaged by the proviso to section 63(7) of the , the preference contemplated by the second proviso was not violative of article 14 and had to he struck down. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that (i) the first respondent had an equal chance to get a permit even on inter state route or notified area; (ii) the fourth respondent had been denied the benefit of the second part of the proviso; and (iii) the third respondent had not been able to get the certificate of the approval from Central Government because of the rule of priority envisaged by section 63 (7). Dismissing the appeals, this Court. HELD: 1. The scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permit for stage carriages and contract carriage permits is very obviously the promotion of tourism and the approval of the Central Govern ment would be given to those operators of tourist cars and travel agents who may be expected to serve that purpose. [1019C] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , followed. Sher Singh 's case, overruled. Sher singh 's decision in Sher Singh was not correct. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka Road Transport Corpora tion and the private operators who did not get a certificate from the central Government, because of its rule of precedence contained in proviso to Section 63(1) of . [1010F] Sher singh vs Union Of India, , followed and applied. Sher Singha Singh vs State of Punjab, ; and Sher Singh & Ors. vs Union Territory of Chandigarh, ; referred to.

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant. The business was transferred to the respondent and the respondent paid some amounts towards sales tax. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the business. The respondent contended that the State Government had no authority under its rule making power under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the, business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay sales tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. The High Court held that Rule 21 A was ultra vires and the State Legislature had no power under its Rule making power to create the transferee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 23A was beyond the rule making powers of the State Govt. under section19(1). HELD: (i) The word 'assessment ' in the scheme of sales tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. As the Judicial Committee observed in Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; , that Rule 22A is beyond the Rule making powers, the State Govern ment has no authority to enact the rule. [665 E F] (ii) The High Courts have not erred in holding that Rule21 A was intra vires of the rule made by the State. The rule cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10(1), because, it is beyond question whether there is a liability created inter se between the State and the transferee on the one hand and the transferor on the other. [664 F G] Badrida Daga vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, ; and Badridash Daga vsC.I., Bihar; , , referred to. (iii) Rule 21A is ultra vires of rule making authority of the Government under section 9(1)(c). The High court was right in holding the rule valid. [663 G] (iv) Rule 23 A is beyond its rulemaking power of the state Government either under section 10 or section 19 (2)(C) of Act. It was then submitted that it was not open to the State government to rely on the instrument inter vivos between the transferor and the transfer, and to contend that there was no liability created in the transferor 's name.

The appellant was appointed senior jailor, Surendranagar District Jail. On March 6, 1953, the respondent Accountant General of Prisons, Saurashtra, served a charge sheet on him under section 4(1) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, alleging that while he was serving at Surendaranagar District, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The respondent pleaded guilty and pleaded that the charge was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy of the report of enquiry held against him, amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of Constitution and dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that there had been breach of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution as the respondent was not supplied with a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but pleaded that it was not necessary to supply copy of such report. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the omission on the face of the enquiry held by the Enquiry Officer amounted to denying reasonable opportunity to the Government servant and that the respondent had failed to prove his case. [923 D] The State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , followed. In the present case, the appellant was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State of Maharashtra and the respondent. The State had the report before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the enquiry officer were bound to influence him. [936 D] In the instant case, there was no duty cast upon the competent authori ty to provide him with a certified copy of his report. He could not have given a copy thereof as earnings under a concurrent contract of service. The High court was right that the appellant had failed and neglected to supply a copy. [981 E] State of West Bengal vs Abdul Kabir, ; and Terrell vs Secretary of State for the Colonies, , referred to. In view of the fact that the enquiry report was not furnished to the respondent, the order of the High court decreeing payment of arrears of salary is truly a liability. The decree of the trial Court decreeing payment was truly a likeness in respect thereof and it was therefore entitled to give relief to him. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed.

The appellants were the owners of a coal mine. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the said land on the allegation that the appellant had encroached upon it and had rendered the remaining coal liable to be removed under the previous lease in favour of the appellants. The trial court held that the respondent had encroached on the land and passed an order for the value thereof by way of damages. On appeal, the High Court accepted the finding of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts in India had wrongly decided the question whether the respondents had knowledge of the trespass only within three years of the suit and not within three year in the circumstances of the case, and that the finding was vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the onus of proving the knowledge of his father wag on the respondents to prove that he had knowledge about the encroachment only within 3 years of his coming into possession and that it was not permissible for a court to reconstruct the plan with reference to revenue records when the plan is self contained and drawn to scale. [501 D] (ii) The onus of proof in the former sense is on the party who comes to Court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. In the present case, the burden was upon the appellant to prove the fact that the knowledge was within three yea years of its purchase and not beyond three years. [500 E] (iii) The burden of proving that the information given by the respondents was false lies on the plaintiff who asserts a right and it may be having regard to the circumstances, of each case, that the facts proved were not in his knowledge or belief. But the question is whether they have adduced evidence which had the effect of shifting the onus. [50 F] (iv) The presumption under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act is that the burden in the first sense is upon the party to prove affirmatively that the suit is within time. Under section 101 of the Evidence Act, the onus is on him who comes before the Court to got a decision of the existence or otherwise of the fact which he asserted. In other words, it is for him to prove his knowledge of facts on a particular date, for the said fact would be within his peculiar knowledge. [51 F H] (v) The question is one of fact and not of law. It is well settled that a map or plan prepared by a party cannot be used as evidence indicating thereby that it is the duty of a plaintiff to establish at any rate prima facie that the land is within 3 yea, prior to 1932. [52 F H; 53 A] (vi) The fact that in the plaint the defendants had not denied the fact was not sufficient to prove its effect. In such a case, there could be no doubt that the plaintiff had knowledge and had knowledge thereof. But it was for him who brought the suit to recover the specific moveable property or for compensation. [53 C D] Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, Pat. 75 I.A. 206, approved. (vii) The finding of fact arrived at by the courts below that the respondents were aware of the encroachment on the appellants ' land only in 1941 was not correct. The High Courts had rightly decided the matter and the findings must be set aside. [54 F] Talwarkhan Vagra & Ors., Pat. 751, approved and followed.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the order of discharge passed under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry was justified or not. Held, that the employer could defend the action under r., 18 (a) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action taken under r, 18 (b) was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power conferred on it under that rule. The appellant had failed to satisfy the Tribunal when it came to the conclusion that the exercise of power was bona fides and was mala fide. The Tribunal had rightly held that the order terminating the services of the appellant was bona bonafide and was therefore invalid. The Chartered Bank, Bombay vs The Chartered bank Employees ' Union, ; , referred to. Held further, that in a case where the termination of service is capricious, arbitrary or unnecessarily harsh on the part of the employer judged by normal standards of a reasonable man that may be cogent evidence of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The fact that the misconduct was proved did not justify an inference that there had been in fact mis conduct. The Industrial Tribunal had no power to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of the service under r 18 (c). The appellant could not rest its case merely on r.18 (a), and it could not be said that the tribunal had gone wrong in holding that the action was bona bona fide. Held also, that there is no constitutional provision in the Industrial Disputes Act which requires a proper enquiry to be made before an industrial tribunal for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. The employer could not therefore contend that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to inquire whether the action of the employee was a colourable exercise or not and it was not open to the Tribunal to go into the circumstances of the case as to whether there was any misconduct on the record. The respondent had been given an opportunity to show cause against the dismissal order, but he did not avail himself of that opportunity. The enquiry was held by the appellant in a bona fide manner and the tribunal rightly held it to be a colourable one. The appeal must accordingly fail.

The appellant was the receiver of a theatre belonging to the respondent. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that as sub lessee or licensee under law it was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the cinema, and that the respondents were estopped from denying its rights to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. [445 B] (ii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court has recorded a finding that the agreement dated December 1, 1960 created a lease and that it was not even averred that it had been a lease. The High Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Court and which could not be decided by the High court until the parties had opportunity to lead oral evidence thereon. [441 G H] (iii) The High court has recorded findings that the appellant was entitled under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 to obtain an order for exhibiting exhibit motion picture in the cinema theatre under the agreement. [442 C D] (iv) The trial Court had not decided any issues at all. It had also held that the question asked in cross examined by the appellant did not decide any issue at that stage. The Trial Judge was therefore right in holding that the questions asked were already concluded by the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960. [443 D E] (v) The order passed by the trial Court is set aside and the Trial court is directed to dispose of the suit. [444 F G] (vi) The appeal must be dismissed. [44 C] (vii) The respondent 's application for permission to exhibit a document was not barred by the principle of res judicata because a consent decree was merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the Court. A consent decree, according to law, must be held to create a bar of resjudicata as far as the question of document of November 27, 1954, creatin g a lease is concerned. [45 D E].

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was confirmed on 30.8.1979. The appellant, who was an officer of the Indian Army, was granted permanent commission in the I.A.F.I. for a period of one year w.e.f. 1st March, 1983. On 20th August, 1979 he was declared unfit by a medical board and was re instated from I.P.S. to the post in question on 30th August 1985. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his order of termination which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of appointment could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be allowed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The order of the High court dated 24th March, 1988 directing that the respondent was entitled to salary upto 30th of August 1985 if the order was found to be an invalid one. It is on this basis that the High Courts while setting aside the order by its order dated 24.3.1988 directed that the respond ent was entitled for salary upto the period he was entitled. The High Court had, therefore, rightly held that the termination order could not he sustained and directed the respondent to be reinstated in service. [243D E] 1.2. The fact that no order of extension had been sanctioned by the Governor beyond 30th September, 1985 would not make out that the respon dents had put forward at that stage such a case. His only case was that the interim order that had been passed on 10.7.86 entitled him to be re instate in service even though there was no order from extension of service. If the respondent is really aggrieved by the Judgment dated 24/3.88 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that he did not do but on the other hand he proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be reinstatement in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. [245E F] 1:3. The direction given by the High COurt was wholly unsustainable. [246B] 2.1 The respondent was employed only under a contract which specified the term of his appointment which extended only upto 30.08.1985. Since it is admitted that no orders of extension have been sanctioned, the respondent could not claim to be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. [244E F; 244A] 2:2. In the instant case, the HighCourt was right in disposing of the Writ petition on 24. 3.1988 declaring that the Respondent was entitled tO salary upto 31st August, 1985.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not sufficient to convict him as there was no motive for the murder and his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The discrepancies in the evidence were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the Sessions Judge. [368E] 2. It is obvious that the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thougly thoust that an order of conviction could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial or compelling reasons". However, the circumstances were such as would show that the witnesses had been subjected to cross examination which was not suggested by the prosecution that the accused made a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased. The evidence of P. Ws. 1 to 3 and the evidence given by them was corroborated by the evidence on record. [369F G] 3. The fact that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have been received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused. The injury must have been caused in the manner suggested by P.W. 3 and he had no doubt that he must have taken fanciful possibilities to deflect the course of justice. If two reasonably probable and evenly balanced views of the evidence are possible, one must necessarily concede the existence of a reasonable doubt. But, fanciful and remote possibilities must be left out of account. To entitle an accused person to the benefit of a doubt arising from the possibility of a duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him. If the preponderance of probability is all one way, a bare possibility of another view will not entitle the accused to claim the benefit thereof. [370E F] 4. The appellant was entitled to the benefits of doubt arising out of the injuries suffered by him. He was entitled only to the advantage of any doubt. It was not necessary for him to entitle an acquittal person to claim that benefit of any doubts. It could be claimed in the facts and circumstances of this case. [371F G]. Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , Bhim Singh Rup Singh vs State Of Rajasthan, A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460, Bhim Singh, Rup Singh & Anr. vs The State of Punjab, ; and Khem Karan & Ors., vs State, of U.P., ; , referred to.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge in the High Court of Madras. He was given the power to appoint Judges of the High Courts and the High court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The President of India, however, issued an order dated September 27, 1979 appointing a Judge for the purpose of removal of a Judge from his office. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution as he was not given the first opportunity to be heard before the order of removal was passed. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the President had no power to remove a Judge either of the Judges or of the Chief justice of a High Court and that the second opportunity to make an application for prosecution under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 was not available to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to grant sanction for prosecution of a judge of the Delhi High Court; (ii) the provisions of section 6 (1)(C) of Act 1 of 1947 are applicable only to a Judge who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his duties under article 124(4); and (iii) the power of removal under section 7 of the Act is not available for prosecution for an offence punishable under section 5 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of clause (e) of sub section (1) of section 5 are applicable to a person who is appointed in connection With the affairs or administration of the State and cannot be prosecuted without sanction under section 4(2). [236D] 2. The word "court" in clause (c) has to be given its widest connotation so as to include judges of the highest status, even though they are not removable by the wide definition of the expression in the Act but whose category for the grant of sanction is not envisaged by section 6 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [236E] 3. The words "courts" and "other authorities" used in clause(e) have to be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. In the case of Judges of High Courts, and Judges of other High Courts the provisions contained in clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 have to he given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under section6. [237E F] 4. The expression "court ' has been defined in clause 2(a) to mean a court having jurisdiction over any matter pending before it and includes a Judge or a Judge not removable therefrom by or with the sanction of Central Government. The term "court " is used in cl. (e), which means an appellate Court, and includes the HighCourt. [238F] 5. The power to punish a judge under section 3(1) is conferred on the President of the States and the Supreme Courts are invested with the same powers as are vested in the Central Government by the Constitution. The conferment of such power is not contemplated by section 2(c). It is for this reason that the word "Court" has to mean the Court competent to appoint and to grant permission for prosecution. [239H; 240A] 6. The constitutional functionaries, while dealing with the allegations of corruption against a superior Judge and the special law enacted by Parliament under Article 124(5) are clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office in the Union or State. [240B C] 7. The Constitution, while providing that their position would be akin to that of a Chief Justice, has not laid down any specific provision for the Act.

The appellant was a member of the Sahas ' community. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were born in the said constituency. The contestants at the election held on various grounds including the Saha 's caste, subcastes, etc., claimed to be a member thereof as a member. The Tribunal rejected this claim holding that the appellant belonged to the "Kolri" community which was a Scheduled Caste and not a member belonging to the Schedule Caste specified in item 40 of the Presidential List of 1950. The High Court held that the said entry was not a sub caste within the Sunri caste group within the meaning of section 2(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had gone wrong in considering the Saha s 's claim to be an independent caste. [391 C] (ii) The finding that Sahas were a wholly independent caste was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue. Evidence could alter the natural interpretation of the words in the Order. For the same reason, the correct interpretation of item 40 was that it indicates men of the Sunari District and those parts of the Purnea District which had been transferred to West Bengal were not to be considered as belonging to a Scheduled caste. That would show that where the exclusion is by a test other than a caste group, the Order expressly says so. It is natural to think that if the excluded Sahas are those Sunri sity members within the same kind, they would have said so; it would then have read " Sunri excluding those who bore the surname Saha". [391 G H] (iii) The High Courts were in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as they appear to have done. [392 C D] (iv) The view of the High Court that the Saha S 's family belongs to a smaller caste group is incorrect. If the intention was to exclude from Sunri community those members of that caste who bore tho surname, the order would have made that clear. In the absence of such words "urg" must be understood as referring to a larger caste group of Sunri Caste.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building in which he had a share. The landlord filed a complaint against the appellant under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a sum of Rs. 30,000 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture and the deposit of Rs 27,500 as consideration. The Magistrate convicted him under section 19(2) of that Act and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs 30,0001. On appeal by the appellant the High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave it was contended that the offence arose only when the complainant paid the sum of money in respect of the furniture, and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to try the case. Held, that the words "the relinquishment of his tenancy of any premises" in section 19 (1) (c) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates control Act, LVII of 1947, were not used in the Transfer of Property Act but only meant for the transfer by a tenant of his interest which was made unlawful under section 15 of that act. The words " the relinquishment of tenancy of an tenancy ofany premises" occurring in section 108(1)(c) did not occur in the transfer of the tenancy and therefore the offence under section 16 of the Act arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition of the lease. The word "relinquishment" does not occur to the transfer, but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are sections which deal with the relinquishment. In the present case the transaction was not one to the lessor and the surrender was made by the tenant for the purpose of making necessary words in the lease, and the appellant could not be convicted under section19(2). The word 'relinquishes or gives up of possession in general terms. The intention of the legislature to the transferred a lease by sub letting is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. In view of the fact that the word "related" does occur in section 17(1), the conviction under section 20(2)(a) cannot be sustained.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It had its factory at the time of the agreement with the appellant and as their demands were not accepted, the Government made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication. The Tribunal took note of the various factors which were required to be taken into consideration in arriving at its conclusion that the company was in an extremely high scale and it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden. It also observed that the dearness allowance would be available only on a slab system, and that it would be difficult for the company to bear such a situation. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Tribunal, Maharashtra, contending that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable and in any event in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January, 1976, when the workmen had been given the benefit of the new scale. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the new scheme was not fair and justified on the ground that it modifies the original award dated 20th December 1978 and the corrigendum made consequent thereto is also quashed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that having regard to the financial capacity of the appellant, the Tribunal erred in making the wage scales retrospective and in making its wage scales retrospectively effective from 1st February, 1976. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The award was made on December 20, 1978. On December 22, 1978 that is to say, two days after the Award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was not clearly mentioned in the award that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. Since there was to be a flat increase of Rs., 150/ in that scale, the order dated December 22. 1978 of the Tribunal was made in accordance with the directions given by this Court. [178C D] 2. The basic and basic question considered by the Industrial Court was whether the corrigendum was in effect a fresh award. It is clear from the reference order that the Tribunal had not taken into account the financial capa tion of the appellants, but it was only one increase contemplated in the Award. The additional financial liability was considered to be Rs. 50/ and the individual workmen raised an objection that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat rate of Rs 150/ to each workman in the category of Draftsmen and Rs 100/ to all other workmen in their basic pay. It was also contended that the corrigendum had no application to the cost of living index. The appellants filed an application before the Tribunal for correcting the award so as to bring out what was intended. [179D E] 3. The amendment made by the Tribunal is not a fresh one and it cannot be said that an illegality warranting interference under Article 136 is committed if some other method is adopted. The tribunal has given satisfactory reason for adopting a different mode and there is no ground for quashing the order of the tribunal. [180F G] 4. The corrigendum was made by mistake in paragraph 22 of award, which is as follows: "The existing pay scales of Rs 50/ to Rs. 200/ per month are fixed at the step higher in the revised scale. However, the additional load factor is being allowed in the basic pay packet whereas the junior employees would get a large benefit. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they surely would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them That was why the Tribunal thought that an all round flat increase in the general pay scales is being made to meet the demands of the employees. None of these alternatives were actually adopted by the appellant. The fact that the workman raised industrial disputes regarding his claim for dearness allowance was not known to the appellant at any time and the same was submitted (vide para 23 of award). [180G H; 181A] 5. The main question considered in the appeal is whether the amendment result in the insertion of a new scale would yield but a very small and almost a token increase in his size of pay packet while fixing the basic salary of each employee.

The respondent, an award made by the Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. The appellant contended before the High Court that section 15 of the Act was inapplicable because the wages prescribed by it were not payable under any award or settlement between the parties or order of a court, and that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. Held, that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, are applicable to the case as the wages fixed by the Award did amount to wages as defined by section 2(vi) of the , and it also argued that the wages payable under an award could not be included in the definition of wages prescribed under section 2 (vi). The provisions of section 2 of the Bombay Act were applicable only to the wages which were fixed by an award. Section 2(iv) as it stood at the relevant time provided, inter alia, that any remuneration payable under a award or settle ment between the employer and his employees shall be included therein in the main definition under section2 (vi), and that, therefore, the wages structure prescribed was not a contract of employment. The provisions contained in sections 23 and 29 were applicable to cases where no such scheme or procedure had been prescribed by them. The award did not amount to a contract as defined in section 2.(vi) and it could not take in the wages under section 25(1). The Bombay High Court was right in holding that the application made by it was competent for the Industrial Tribu nal to entertain the application. The Bombay and Calcutta High Courts had held that the applications made by respondents were incompetent under section 15, of the . [421 D E] The Bombay decision in the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 15, approved. The fact that section 2)(vi) was not applicable to a case where no change or revision of the terms appears to be justified, would not justify the application of the wages for the period during which it remained binding on the parties. [422 D E].

The appellant was a Sub Assistant Surgeon in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was entrusted with the work of obtaining signatures or thumb impressions of the employees before wages were paid to them. The sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 409 and the Chief Secretary, Home Department sent a communication to the appellant that he had been "directed to convey sanction of the Government to his prosecution". The Chief Secretary sent a reply to the letter. The Chief Secretaries sent a telegram to the effect that he did not receive the amount in question and that by this expedient he received Rs. 51 as gratification from the employees employed in the works, and that he misappropriated the same. The appellant contended that the prosecution was bad for want of sanction under s. 197(l) of Code of criminal Procedure. Held, that the sanction under sec. 197 (1) was necessary before the appellant could be prosecuted under section409, and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the entrustment and/or dominion over property by a public servant whether sanctioned or not must depend on the facts of each case. The question whether sanction is necessary for prosecution under s 197(i) will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each particular case. In the present case, the elements alleged against the second accused were, first, that there was an "entrustment" and/and/or 'discharged by the appellant, secondly, that he retained money in his capacity as a public servants; thirdly, that it was not necessary to obtain sanction under S. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code for prosecuting him under section 120B, I.P.C., and lastly, that no sanction was required for prosecution thereunder. The absence of sanctice was fatal and the conviction should be quashed. The conviction should therefore be set aside. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. The acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate was illegal. The High Court had rightly held that the appellant did not claim to have paid the amount to the second respondent, and as such no sanction under Sec. 197 was necessary. The prosecution was therefore quashed. It was not a case where the appellant was charged with criminal misappropriation or forgery.

The appellant was a banking company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State. The income tax authorities determined its assessable income under the Travancore Income tax Act, 1922, but did not include the loss from the branch situate outside the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred in British India under section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, from the profits accruing or arising in British Indian State; and (ii) that the first proviso to section 24 (1) Of the Indian Incometax Act, which applied only to business carried on by an assessee in BritishIndia was not applicable to the head "business" in the present case. Held: (i)(a) The words "any other purpose" in section 10 of the Travancore Act were wide enough to include the income of an assessee for all purposes as well as income arising outside British India and therefore it necessarily applied to the Head "business " in the two territories, i.e., British India, and the loss under that head could not be deducted from profits made in British British India or in the case of Travancore State in British Columbia Railway Co. vs Bezwada Municipality (1946) L.R. 233 I.A. 271, relied on. (b) The first proviso was applicable only to a business carried out by an assesses in British Pakistan and not to any other section. The second proviso to the section did not apply to a case where the loss sustained was a loss of profits or gains which would be taxable in India under the Indian Act. (ii)(a). The expression "business in British Parliament" in article 12 means business in British or State in respect of all income, profits and gains accruing or arise in British territory or in an Indian State. (iii)The second proviso was not a modification of the substantive provisions of section 24 of the Income tax , which provided that where the assessee sustained is a loss in profits and losses of a business or vocation to which the first Proviso to sub section (1), is applicable, and, if the income and gains of that business, profession or vocation are under the provisions of clause (c) of sub section 2, exempt from tax such loss shall not be set off against profits and gain accruing or arose in British. (iv)The third proviso was a modification to the second proviso by providing that where a loss sustained is one of profits and income which is taxable in British rupees but which was not received or brought into Indian State in the previous year by or on behalf Of the assessee or were brought into the respective territories, but this income, if any, (1)[1955] 1 S.C.R., 869, 869. arising in India or other Indian States) was exempt from payment of tax such losses shall not exceed the amount of loss set off under section 4(3).

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence corroborating the other evidence already against him was a piece Of evidence which connecting him with the dacoity and looted the property. [724 D E] (ii) If the gap of time is too large, the presumption that the accused was concerned with the murder itself may be drawn. It is not necessary to state categorically in this case that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of by receivers till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [700 E F] (iii) The fact that the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market does not make any difference. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime is made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap is too small, the finding is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants or to have left the goods in their custody till suchtime as the Original offenders could have taken them away.[724 G H] (iv) The evidence particu larly does not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case. [624 D] (v) If, therefore, the gap was too large to the way as to how the presumption may be made. it is not sufficient to state specifically in this Case that the person with whom the goods were found was the dacoits themselves. This presumption has been drawn and in our opinion rightly in this ease. [650 D] The fact of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to the traders does not lead to the conclusion that they were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits. It was legitimate therefore to raise the presumption in this respect that the persons with whom tho goods were recovered were the dacoity themselves. [625 E F].

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'Tolinner ' within the meaning of Section 5 of the , sought to challenge the vires of section 5 of t he Act on the ground that the section gave an unguided, unchanalised and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. The petitioners contended that since the Act was a Central enactment it was possible of unjust and unjustified discrimination between the two manufacturers and their products, and that the impugned notification was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned Notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223E] 1.2 The provisions in neither section 2 nor the State Act are hit either by any provi sions of Article 14 or Article 15 of the Constitu tion. [222F] 1:3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as an poison for sale, and the substance would not come within Rule 2(x)(2). [223G] 1 :4. The provisions are hit in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This posi tion is well settled and it would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [225A] 1 .5. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale and the sale of a specified poison for consumption and sale thereof. It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and safety of society in view o f the rampant use and sale. [226B C] 1 6. The State Government may by rule regulate the import, possession or sale of any specified poison in any local area in which the use of such poison forthe purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possess ing of the said poison desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. It has become a notorious fact, which is not disputed by its own inherent qualities, or destroying life. [227C D] 1 7. The law in so far as it relates to the interpretation of the provisions of section 2(3) of the Act impliedly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as unclaimed and unchanging. It states that the State Govern ment may by Rule regulate the possession for sale or sale to be regulated in the interest of health and fire safety of the society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the .

The appellant firm was carrying on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee firm had dealings with the benefits of partnership, each with a firm known as M/s. Bhojaji Sobhachand, partners of which the appellant was the father of the firm. In the books of account of the appellants which were maintained by the Income tax Officer in the year of account ending on October 31, 1951, the amount due to the assessee was shown as a bad debt written off as irrecoverable in the books. The Income tax officer disallowed the claim holding that the debt did not arise in the course of money lending business and that the transaction was mere accommodations which could have no bearing to the regular business carried on by the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner agreed with the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the debts were mere accommoda tion which can have no impact on the regular course of business carried out by the appellant and therefore the debt was not one incurred in the ordinary course of its business. The High Court also rejected the assessee 's contention that the amount in question was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending, business or the money lending. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in disallowing a sum of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the asses see in their books of accounts as irrecoverable is not a mixed question of law and fact. [419 D] (2) The finding that the monies sent by the assesses to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the normal course of the money lent business, nor in respect of any other business of the assessee, was correct. [420 E F] (3) The Tribunal had found that the moneys sent by it were not loan made in its ordinary course and in respect thereof the manner in which the partner of the appellant firm tried to explain the position in March 1954 and the stand of the department was that the money was not loans, but a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. [416 G] (4) The conclusion reached by the Tribunal is correct. It is true that the tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar, has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot be denied that the findings reached by it are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The petitioners filed petitions in this Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that they had not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act. This Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the petitioners that as the awards in these cases have not been made within one year from September 20, 1984, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed and therefore, they were not entitled to be made within three years from the date of publication of the declaration. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these special leave petitions. [565E] 2. The facts of the case are highly material and there is no reference in the Special leave petitions to any to the stay order and it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material. [566F] 3. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time was a matter of direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. If he fails to do so, and suppresses material facts his application is liable to be dismissed. [567G H] 4. The High Court granted stay of the further proceedings. Whatever the ultimate effect of the order was highly important in the deter mination of these Special Leave petitions, it cannot be rejected on the grounds that the non production of the very same certainly amount to suppression. [568A B] 5. If the respondents fail to do any thing and suppress material facts, his application was liable to he dismissed. The special leave Petitions are accordingly dismissed. No costs. [569C D] 6. The Special Leave Petition is dismissed. (567D) 7. The petitioner has approached this Court for such relief by way of interim stay. Whatever be the ultimate consequence of the High Court 's order, in view of the provisions contained in Section 11 A of the land Acquisition Act to which we have already referred earlier, it is not necessary to issue notice to the respondents to file their counter affidavit.

The appellant bank claimed that under cl. (ii) of the Sastry award the adjustment basic pay in the new scale should be as on January 1, 1959 and not on January 31, 1959. The appellant contended that the words "subject to rules (i) to (iii) " in cl. 2(a) of para. 5(1) of its Sastry Award were wide enough to include in the definition of "on January 1. 1962" the expression subject to r. 4(a). Held, that the appellant bank 's case was not covered by cl. 3(a), (b) and (c) of Para. 5. The adjustment basic salary as on February 1, 1962 was Rs. 2,000 and the appellant was entitled to two increments under sub cls. (a) and(b). The appellant bank had been given a benefit of the new scales for that area and therefore the adjustment in the Sastry Award was not justified. Prakash Chand Mehra vs Chand Mehra, ; , followed. In the matter of adjustment, all efficiency bars, whether in the previously existing or in the scales provided by the Sastry Act, as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal 's award as modified or the maximum of that scale or the actual basic pay as on 1st January 1959, as the case may be, should be given over and above what has been worked out under sub cl. 5, are subject to cl. 4 (a). The fact that by oversight sub cl.(d) of el. (iv) was not made a separate clause would make no difference for sub cl (b), because the adjustment of the appellant 's basic pay had to be given after adjustments have been made under sub clauses (a),(b) or (c). In the present case, the appellant Bank 's claim was based on two different verbal changes in the Desai award and the workmen were entitled to increments as provided in sub cls.(a), and (b). There is no dispute that by mistake sub cl(i) of cl. I had been introduced in the award as amended by the labour Appellate Tribunal. The fact, however, that by inadvertence sub cl, (iii), was not incorporated would make any difference for the purpose of cl.(iv) of sub cls (a); and the fact that the workman 's pay as at the time of his appointment had been IV of the scales fixed under the Sastry awards scale equal to or next above his basic pay, could not be taken into consideration.

The appellants, who were owners of a plot of land in 1854, applied for the allotment of a five star hotel. The Director of the Zoo, after considering the objections filed by the appellants, recommended to the State Government that the land should be relinquished in favour of the appellants. The Minister for Urban Development submitted a note to the Chief Minister on June 29, 1981 stating that the Hastings House property may be offered to the I.T.D.C., and the Begumbari land may be given to the Taj Group of Hotels. The Lt. Governor forwarded his reply pointing out that the said proposal was not acceptable to the Zoological Department because the Hub Group of hotels had no access to the said plot of lands. The Col lector, on receipt of this note, wrote to the Secretary of the Ministry of Housing and Veterinary Services, stating that it would be willing to buy the land, he asked for a suitable Committee to consider the matter and submit its report. On June 29 1981, the Director of Zoo had submitted a Note to the C.D., stating that if the Hqrs. wanted to buy this land, the question of allotting the same to the T.T., will be relinquished. The appellants ' request was rejected by the Minister for Metropolitan Development on the ground that the Zooron and the Hodgs. were not acceptable by the Government. The matter was taken up by the Cabinet and the Government of West Bengal appeared to have been on the search for two suitable plots of land which could be offered only to the Indian Red Cross Society, and the Col lege of Hotels who considered it necessary to negotiate with them in regard to the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The Committee was of the view that the facilities available in the Hundies would be left unprovided for if the land was given to a foreign company. The Government of India appeared before the Cabinet on June 28, 1981 and the Cabinet approved the proposal to lease out the Begumpet land to the five star hotels. On July 29,1981, the Chief Secretary sent his reply stating that there were already in existence a number of multistoreyed buildings all around the Zurich Hotel and that the Taj group of Hotels had been given the right to sell the land. The Hub group of hotels filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the decision of the Cabinet. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the decision taken by the Ministry was perfectly bona fide and that it was not forgotten that if it was assumed that the Government had the power to transfer the land to Taj Group, the Government did not have the power under the Land Ceiling Act to transfer it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were in error in holding that there was no need to mention the needs and interests of the Government; that the policy decision of Government was not taken by it at all; that it had been taken into account and irrelevant considerations had been ignored; that if a public auction or a private company was to be offered a particular industry, separate provision would have to be made for them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The policy decision no doubt has not been observed in the letter of the Director General of Zoology dated June 29. 1981 but it is clear that it is not forgotten whether the Government was aware of the question as to what was involved in the proposal for lending over a piece of land to respondent No. "the Hasting" of Hotels, and that what was really involved here was not the sale of the land but a lease by the Govern ment. [260F G] 2. The provisions of the Bengal Public Parks Act, 1904 vested the Hestment Authority with the power of the Committee of Management to deal with the land in any manner that they liked. It is difficult to understand how the provisions of this Act have any relevance to the question. The Act has no application to the Hortune Park and it was only when the Hutments House property was put up for sale that would result in an unhealthy atmosphere for the animals and the members of the Hooghly Club, and therefore, the Holacars were not heard in the matter before the decision was taken. [262H; 263A B] 3.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had a cash balance of Rs.4,299 in the books of M/s. Pearls & Beads. The assessee had a large cash balance with him and had also a sum of Rs,50,000 to his son. The Income Tax Officer, who was of the view that the said amount should be included in the net wealth of the assessee, issued notices under section 10(1) of the Act calling upon the assessee to debit his account to the extent of Rs 1,50 lakhs and credit the respective amounts in the names of the aforesaid persons. The respondent contended that there was no valid gift of Rs 25,000 by him to his sons and therefore the amount had been wrongly included in his net wealth by the Income Tax officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee did not make a valid gift but only oral instructions were given to the assessee and that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the donor by reason of which he could make the gift by such book entries. On appeal, the High Court held that there had been no valid gifts. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that there is no valid transfer of the principal amounts as there was a valid transfer and the interest paid in respect of the accounts standing in the name of the donees was allowable as a deduction in the hands of the asses see. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [130D] 2.1 In order to decide whether the assessee had made a valid gifts or trust in respect thereof, the Income tax Officer must have regard to the facts and circumstances of each case other than those of the factum of gift, it could not be said that the donee had not retained the possession and enjoyment of the property to the entire exclusion of the donee or to the whole exclusion of his donor. [131E] 2:2 In the instant case, the assessee was the karta of a Hindu Undivided Family. On 20th November, 1956, the assesseee made a gift of certain amounts by way of gift in his favour and the gift was effected by debiting the assessee 's account in the firm and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. The sums were en tained in the account books of the Hindu undivided Family with the amount shown in the accounts regularly for some time, until a bank from which C had obtained an overdraft objected to such crediting of interest. On a reference made by the High court, the question was whether there was valid gift or trust. [132G H] 2(a) The assessee was not appearing when the money was transferred by debit ing the assessee. It was only oral instruction given to him to make a proper gift. The accounts were not maintained in the records of the company. The amounts were not available with the assessee for the amount in question on that date. [133B] (b) The High court was in agreement with the Tribunal and it held that section 10 did not apply to the gifts made by transfer in the assessee firm by debitings in the balance sheet. There was no evidence of acceptance of entries made in the book of account and by the declaration, nor any such entry was made in his books of account. [134C] (c) The Tribunal had correctly held that under section 123 of the , in case of gift of movable property, the transfer may be effected by delivery. In that view of the matter, except to the limited extent indicated above, the entries in the return books could not effectuate gifts. As the respondent was not present when the amount was transferred to the account of C and the assessee could make a gift by book entries might or might not have been possible for the assessee or the family or a company which was not a banking company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid gifted. [135E F] (d) The order and judgment of the High Courts are set aside and the case remitted to the Tribunal for fresh disposal according to law.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 were framed by the State Government under article 309 of the Constitution. Under Rule 3(1) of the said Rules the Governor is empowered to appoint a person as the Chief Justice of the High Court and to add or sub cadre to the cadre of district judges. The rules provided that the Chief justice shall be the sole authority to effect the necessary transfers. The State Government was directed by the High court to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts as District Judges or Additional District Judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts for three years or more. The High Court took a policy decision that as a general rule judicial officers should be posted at the place of their choice, the Chief Secretary was to act as the head of the subordinate judiciary and the administrative remembrance and member sales tax tribunal were constituted. In view of this policy the Chief Secretaries of the State Governments were requested to implement the orders in question on the very day the decision was rendered. The Government of Orissa by its letter dated April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to the implementation of the orders of transfer ordered by the said High Court. On March 6, 1967 the High Courts of Assam and Orissa passed a resolution to the effect that as the power to transfer District Judges was exclusively vested in the Chief Minister, the State should not be transferred to the High Commissioner for administrative reasons. The Governor accordingly issued an order transferring the three officers mentioned above to other posts. The appellant who was working as a Superintendent and legal remembrancer in the High Judicial Service filed a writ petition before the High COurt challenging the orders transferring him from one post to another. The learned Single Judge of the Orissa High Court held that the transfer was not in accordance with law and directed the State of Orissa to implement it. On appeal by special leave, the Division Bench reversed the decision of the single judge and restored the order of transfer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power to appoint District Judges is included in article 235(b) of our Constitution. It was not the case of the parties that he was placed at the disposal of the Government for any definite period. It could not be said that he had no authority to hold the posts in question. [161F] (2) The High Courts were within their powers in posting Shri B.K. Patro, a District and Sessions Judge as the law Secretary. He was only concerned with the appointment, promotion and posting of judicial officers. The cadre of the superior judicial service consisted of not only the posts of district and sessions judges but also officers holding other posts, and one such post could be filled only by the Chief Justices. [162G] (3) The Government had already implemented that part of the order as well. Those officers were now functioning in the posts to which they were transferred. The transfer was therefore illegal. [164A B] (4) The State of West Bengal vs Ranga Mahammad, ; , referred to. (5) The cadre with which the High Judges are concerned is a reference to a cadre consisting essentially of officers under the direct control of the Court. It is in that context that the Court held the transfer of District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre must necessarily be outside the power of the Governor and fall to be made by the order. [165G H] (6) The word "control" in article 236(b), therefore, means control over the officers who preside over those courts. It does not mean that the power is only concerned in the appointment or promotion to a vacancy in the service. The power is not confined to the post of District Judge on the Government but extends to the District Judges and the judicial officers work in the secretariat. [166H] (7) The fact that powers are conferred on them for the good of the public and they should act in such a way as to advance public interest. If they act with that purpose in view as they should, then there is no room for conflict and no question of one dominating the other arises.

The appellant, a co sharer in the State of Haryana, had filed a suit for pre emption against the respondent No. 1 and the co sharers of the vendors. The mother State, the State, had also filed an appeal against the decree passed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if an outsider is introduced as a co co shar holder in a property, it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'other co shari ners ' in clause (fourthly) of section 15(1) of Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 is rendered redundant. [126A] 2. In the present case, the appellant seeks to exercise the right of pre emptor to those relative or relatives of the vendor or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section15(1), even if they happen to be co shar holders. The phrase 'other ' preceding.the word 'co sharer ' is rendered meaningless. [127B] 3. In view of the provisions contained in section 15 (1)(b) and clause fourthly of section, 15( 1)(b), the purport of Atam Prakash 's case was to deny the right to those relatives or relatives who were mentioned in the former first three Clauses of section. The right of preemption is held intra vires the Consti tution. [128C D] 4. In a case where the sale is of a share out of joint land or property, and is not made by all the co co co ments jointly, only the other co sharger and the tenants can exercise the power of pre ap peal in preference for which no justification was found. [129D E] 5. The intention of the legislature was to confer the right on specified family members of the vendee or vendors in the first three clause even if their happen to he co sharees. The Legislature desired to confer such a right on certain persons as well as to the son. The object of the Act was to protect and preserve tenants ' interest in common, and to prevent the concentration of wealth in common; but since this Court found certain intrinsic contradictions in the list of relatives covered by section 15 of the , it upheld the right conferred on co sharants for reasons stated earlier. [130D E]. 6. The purport of the said provision after the preceding clauses was that where the sales were of a joint land, it would make common administration extremely difficult to secure the right in the order of preference conferred on them by that provision. The relations in the present two clauses are not erased from the statute book as unconstitu tional. [131E F]. 7. The purpose of section 12(1 ) (b) is to protect the tenant 's interest in the land and to safeguard the interests of the tenants against exploitation. The rights of pre co shar er are conferred firstly on the lineal descendents of the owner in order of succession; secondly, in the co mittee or vendors ' broth er 's son of the purchaser or vendors; thirdly, in other co co ordinate nesses of the sale or property and is, not made. by all co sharists jointly only the others. [132E F] 8. The language of section 14(1 (b), read with section 15, is clear enough to exclude any speci fied co owners from the scope of clause fourthly. Section 15(2) provides that persons in whom right of Pre empture vests in respect of sales of agricultural land and village immovable property shall vest in the son or daughter 's sons or daughters 's daughter ' or sons 's widow or sons of the pre em ployees. [133G H] 9. The words "other co co share" in clause fourthly conveys the possibility of their being co sharener also. What this Court disapproved is that if the preceding clause were not eroded from the statu tory book as unconstitutional, the word 'other cooperative co sharen ' is struck down as reasonable and in public interest. [134A B] 10. The position of law has been kept in mind by this Court in several decisions.

The appellants, who were the original plaintiffs in a suit for title and injunction, filed an application under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, for possession and injunction. The Trial Court granted a decree for possession of the entire property of the appellants. On appeal, the High Court held that once the court was satisfied that there was a compromise, it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appel lant that the alienees had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and the alienation was not valid and the transferees had become owners of the property and had even maintained that there were agreements for sale prior to compromise. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants have no interest created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In view of the fact that there has been a allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to the alienee, which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too we have no jurisdiction. [541C D] 2.1 A compromise petition is genuine and lawful. The same has to be acted upon. It is lawful the same has been filed in this Court. [542F] 2:2 In view Of the fact, that there is a allegation that the alienation are valid and not binding on the alienor respondent No. 2, the sale deeds are subsequent to 21.8.1987. The alienees have no right created under any alleged sale deed. Their posses sion has become owners ' of the properties and has even maintained the same. [543F] Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108, referred to. 2:3 The alienee has no interest therein in the properties prior to 1.7.1987 and it must hold that the sale deed is subsequent to the said compromise. [544F] 3.1 In view thereof, the suit shall be disposed of and the terms of the compromise shall form part of the order to be drawn up in this court for disposing of the special leave petition.

The appellant company was granted sick leave with effect from December 14, 1969. The workmen were paid dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 900 per month. The company applied for and obtained special leave to appeal as aforesaid. The Industrial Tribunal held that the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick leave are such as to justify rejection of the workmen 's demand and set aside the award in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the benefit of sick Leave granted to the workers should not be extended to the workmen because they had benefited a lot under the entire scheme of the Act and it would not be reasonable and proper to confer any additional benefit on them. HELD: (i) The Industrial Court was justified in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days sick leave at the time of the commencement of the industrial dispute. [83 E] (ii) The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. [84 F G] (iii) The scheme of benefits admissible to the employees under the Industrial Disputes Act is not a bar to the demand of the workman for sick leave. The benefit granted by the Tribunal are not similar to those admissible under section 56 of the , and the workmen would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [85 G H] (iv) The award of the Industrial Court is set aside and the award of benefit of the sick leave granted by it is restored with the modification that the workman shall be entitled to the benefit for the first two days of sickness under the first proviso to section 49 of the . [86 C D] (v) The workmen would get the benefit thereof in addition to the current year 's leave, under a settlement dated July 17, 1969 which is being continued even after the coming into force of the Bombay Industrial Disputes and Conciliation Act, 1947. [87 E F] (vi) The benefits granted by Tribunal are also entitled for the second period of sickness except in the case of continuous illness of the nature mentioned therein, "with regard to a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of ' sickness for which the sickness benefit was last paid. It has to be appreciated that a workman is prevented from earning his normal wages during the period of his illness and there is no justification for the argument that the rate for the benefit at about half his wage, under the award, should be considered sufficient so as to deny him the bene fit of sick leaves on full emoluments during the said period. [86 G H; 86 A B] (vii) The appellant companies are not able to show that the awards in question are illegal or unjust. [88 C D].

The appellant was detained under sub clause (a) of section 3 of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of detention and he filed an affidavit explaining the allegations against him. He also stated that he was not aware of the grounds of his detention as required by section 7 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the grounds did not contain any particulars nor did they state any particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by the petitioner. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The grounds cannot be considered to be vague merely because they are vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation under article 22(5). [391 F] (ii)The question whether or not the grounds furnished were vague must depend on the facts of each case. If the detaining authority is under a constitutional obligation to furnish reasonably definite grounds, as well as adequate particulars then and there, or shortly thereafter. But the right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 21. [391 G] (iii)The requirement of section 7(1) of the . that the ground should be vague must be clearly communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds are furnished. The right of detenue to have a proper representation against his detention cannot be said to be implicit in the language of article 22 (6). [392 G] In the present case there was no reason for the delay in making a proper order.
