The failure to disclose the facts as well, or the ambit and scope of the non disclosure must be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. [392 B C] (iv)The mere fact that the allegations are not as precise and specific as might have been desired does not affect the constitutional right to be afforded a reasonable opportunity to make representation under Article 22(6). The failure of the detaining author to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held as vague. [393 C D] (v)The right of a detenue under article 23(5) includes corresponding obligation on the part of the Government to communicate the decision not to disclose. The requirement of the rule is not merely an obligation on a person to disclose information which is against public interest but also a duty cast upon him by the detaining Authority, not in any other. It follows that the failure to furnish particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against Public interest cannot be regarded as unreasonable.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. He was charged with having committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were that he committed acts prejudicial to the maintenance of discipline, while as a result thereof, he was suspended from service. The Chief of the Army Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry held in his favour and after going into the proceedings, found him guilty of the charges framed against him. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Defence Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r 14 of Army Rules, 1955, was intra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 14 of Indian Army Rules is not ultra vires. It is a rule which is in derogation of section 45 of the . Rule 14 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" it speaks of removal of a person from the service. Section 20 provides that on conviction by Court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. [450 H] (ii) The power under section 19 is an alternative to the power to make rules providing for the removal from the Service of persons subject to the Act. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under, subject to other provisions of the Act, the Central Government may remove a person on the service as undesirable or to suffers such less punishments as is In this Act mention. [451 B C] (iii) The words " subject to" in section 19 make section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Govern ment has no power to remove a persons from the serv ice of any person subject to this Act. Rule 14, therefore, is ultra vires and is not void. [452 E F] (iv) The word "subject" in Section 19 makes it clear that there should be rules and subject to provisions of section 18 and such rules, the central Government may dismiss or remove from the services any person under the service of persons. Rule 15 is a special rule which provides for removal of persons from service under section19 of the read with r.14 of the Indian Railway Establishment Code. [453 E F].

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti under the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958. The respondent filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for a writ quashing the resolution dated February 25, 1963 passed by the Standing Committee on April 1, 1964 and directing that the octroi duty be levied on all goods coming into its local limits as per the Schedule to the Act. The High Court held that the Panchayat could not dismiss the appeal as being barred by limitation because it was filed within 60 days of the date of the resolution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. [217 B] (ii) The resolution dated April 1. 1964 was passed an essential condition precedent to the levy of octroi duty. The Panchayat could validly impose octroi duty and it could be imposed and collected with effect from January 14, 1964. He says that this point was raised before the Full Bench in the case of R.S. Kapur vs State of Punjab ; , and he says that the approval of the Collector on January 14. 1964 relates back to April 1; 1963. [218 C D] (iii) The High court had implied that this decision was not correct because the fixing of the octroi limits with the approval by the Collector is an essential requirement precedent to levy of tax. The Standing Committees were entitled to take action under the Act and the rules. [220 G H] (iv) The scheme of the Fees Rules clearly shows that the general procedure for levying taxes or fees was laid down and then this procedure was made applicable to the imposition of various taxes mentioned in the other parts of the Rules. The scheme is that the General Rules are framed under section 3 of the Bombay Panchayat Act, 1959. [221 A B] The scheme does not require the Panchayat to fix the octroi limit in the resolution passed under r.3(a). The scheme requires the Panchayat and the rate at which it is to be levied. The inhabitants of the village would be entitled to object only to these two matters, namely, (1) the tax or fee imposed and the rates at which they are levied; (2) the rate of tax to be imposed; and (3) the rates fixed by the Municipal Council under r, 4 for all appeals.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be prolonged only when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by the appropriate Government and that as 14 days had expired before March 18, 1952, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the meaning of section 12(6) of the Act. Held, that the provisions of sub section 2 Of section 20 of the , are applicable only when a report is received by an appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings therefore do not end when the reports under section 12 (6) are made by the Conciliation officer but when that report is receives by the Government, the appropriate government has to make its report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the State Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co., Ltd., ; , referred to. The provisions of section 20(2)(b) of Act 2 Of 1952 are applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the Report of the Advisory Officer is received and the report is sent by the Inspector to the appropriate Govern ment. Colliery Labour Union Asanso vs Newerson Bissur Railway Co., , referredto. The Act does not affect the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal under section 20 (2)(a) of that Act. Workers of the Industry Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the industry Colliery, and The Colliery Mazdoor Sabha, Dhanbad, vs Management, of the Institution, approved. Workers ' Union, Asanakulam, Asypereira, , referred. Workers in the Industry colliery Colliery, Nagpur vs Management Of the Industry, and Colliery Mazdoor Union, Dhanbad (A.I.R. 1952 Cal. 941), referred to, Case law reviewed. Workers Union, Colliery Colliery, Ranchi, Asanta Kumar Ghosh vs New beerbhoom Colliery Coal Co. Ltd., , distinguished. The Workers of The Industry Colliery Colliery Colliery Dhanbad, Dhanbad and another vs Management thereof, approved and applied. Workers were not entitled to any relief under section 33 (1) of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the , by an order dated 2nd January, 1983 passed by the respondent No. 1 under section 3(2) of the . The grounds of detention were that on 24th December 1985 between 10th and 11th January 1986 the subject matter of the incident had been referred to a committee constituted for the purpose of enquiry into the exchange of fire between two rival groups. The petitioner was arrested when he was released on bail in pursuance of an order passed by this Court on 2nd February, 1986. On the question whether the detention order was justified or not, HELD: (1) The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. [910C] (2) It is well settled in the constitutional framework that the power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated under the various provisions of different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power to preventive detention should not be exercised. [936F G] (3) The order of preventive detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service of the impugned order was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit filed by the District Magistrate, the detaining authority, it has been stated that the activities of the petitioner 's brother and the petitioner have disturbed the normal tempo of life in Katras and Jogta Police Station in Dhanbad area. The incidents alleged were created a terror and not only law and order problem but problem of public order. [961F G; 910A B] (4) It was also stated that there was a statement to the effect that the petitioner was in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. But on what consideration that opinion was expressed is not indicated especially in view of the fact that the detenu was detained in a murder charge in the background of the circumstances mentioned before. His application for bail could have been opposed on cogent materials before the Court of Justice. [963B C] (5) The detention order, therefore, is set aside.

The respondent assessee firm manufactures gold bars, i.e., manufacturers of shroffs and dealers in gold. The assessee firm manufactured gold bars and sold them to the dealers. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the respondent firm under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 on the ground that it suffered from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator. The High Court struck down sec. 28 of Act, 1969 as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969, constitutionally invalid on the grounds that it suffers from the infirmity of excessive delega tion of legislative powers inasmuch as the restrictions which have been imposed in section 28 are meant to prevent circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object and reasons for exercising the power of discretion conferred on an Administrator by sec. 26(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. [955C] 1.2 In the instant case, the objective, the policy and the scheme of the enactment together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention Of the other provisions is clearly inapplicable. The object, therefore, is not to provide any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. Even the restriction imposed by sec 28 is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry on the business in licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the act in making his orders. [936F G] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise, Poona, ; , followed. 1.3 The object of the Urban Ceiling Act is to provide for the acquisition of goods lending, Banking or any kind of foreign business, for the control of production, manufacture, supply distribution, use and possession of and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. [951B] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthia & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to. 1:4 The object is not the same as the administrator can have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec. 24(6).

The appellants were appointed trustees of a temple by the Manager of a Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, L. R. Act, 1951, in respect of certain properties belonging to the temple. The appellants filed an application before the Magistrate under section 87 of the Act for possession of the properties. The Magistrate held that the lands belonged to the deity and that the alienees had acquired title by adverse possession. On appeal, the High Court held that as the alienors had been appointed trustees, the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the suit could not be governed by article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act; and (ii) the appellants were entitled to a declaration about their title to the properties in question as they had acquired no title by prescription, and that (iii) the High court erred in holding that the suit would be governed only by article 135 B of Indian Limitation. HELD : (i)(a) The suit was not barred by article 136. [133 G] (b) The appellants were not entitled to any declaration as they did not have prescribed title. They had been removed from the properties and other persons had taken up the position as de facto managers, and this position has lasted for more than 25 years. If the alienor was appointed as trustees by the manager on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowment, he could not have filed a suit after 12 years of his appointment. [134 B C] (c) The question as to whether the appellants had acquired any title by res judicata or in any other manner did not arise for consideration because the appellants ' case was covered by article 133 B of that Indian Limitation act. [135 E F] Gnanasambanda vs N. R, Luck. , referred to. (d) The fact that the appellants filed a civil suit on the date when they were appointed trustee did not affect their title. Therefore, the question as regards the adverse possession was irrelevant for the purpose of article 134B. [136 E F]. Gnanasekar vs Natesan Das, L.,R. , applied. (e) The contention that the respondents had been removing the properties from the respective dates of alienations when they became entitled to the property was not correct. [137 B] (f) The title of the alienee is adverse to the appellants and the suit must be dismissed. [138 C D]. G. Narayan Das vs Nityanand Das, I.L.R.

The appellant, who was the owner of a cinema theatre in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the District Magistrate and the appellate authority under the Jammu & Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, so long as there had not been any transfer of the license by the original licensees to another with the sanction of the licensing authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even though the licence had been granted in favour of Ved Gupta and not in favour M/s. Krishan Kumar, the license was still subsisting and that the license had become void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by District Magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema show in the theatre without a licence in contravention of the law. [582B] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding that since the license granted by the licensing authori ty in favour the Apsara Theatre was in favour a partnership consisting of himself and M/S. Krishan Lal and M.L. Sharma, the licensee had no right or interest in the licence which was granted to Ved Gupta in his individual capacity as representing the partnership. [595C D] 2:2 The High COurt has rightly held that the licence is granted for premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the names of the Apnos and Mast Ram Cinema. It is now well settled that where a licence is a grant for the premises and constitutes an interest attached to the premises, it must necessarily follow the title in such building and the cinematograph. [596D E] 2 :3 The High Courts have held that under the provisions of the Act the licence was granted for the property of the firm and therefore the license is valid. [597F G] 2(a) The right to conduct a exhibition of cinematograph films in the cinema by persons other than licensees is vested solely in Ved Gupta, Gupta, the licencee. It cannot be held that it is an interest created in the license.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them, for the purchase of the stock of raw materials, unsold finished goods, spare parts, cars etc. which were in the mills and the factory in question was leased to the appellants for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants were put in possession of the mills on 31 8 1952. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellant under section 12 Of the , terminating the lease, and the appellants filed an application before the respondent for a writ of certiorari for quashing the notice, contending that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section and that the notice was ultra rites. The High Court held that section had no authority under section 10 to issue any directions with reference thereto and that section 10 applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself and that there was no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section that that lease should also have been granted by an evacuee. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 13 Of the Act. Under section 12 of the , the Custodian had the power to cancel a lease granted by him and not to the Custodian. The operative portion of the section which confers power on the Custodian to cancel the lease does not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and cannot prevail as against them and has been inserted ex abundanti cautela. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, , 21 24 S.C.R. 884, followed. (ii) The provisions of section 12 are intended to repel a possible contention that section 13 does not apply to leases granting by the evacuees and cannot override a bar imposed by any law but only applies to leases in respect of which certain directions were given. As Arabinda Ghosh vs Mullick A. Irani, ; , followed. The effect of section 10 is that the Custodian has the power under section 11 to cancel an lease granted to him and he can also be evicted if the Custodian does not exercise his powers under that sub section to cancel such a lease. As saving a possible claim under section 14 does not lie as against the Custodian, and has not been inserted in the section, the respondent was exercising his power under that Section to cancel it.

The respondent was a minor son of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972 determined the ceiling area for the appellant in respect of his father and allotted him to the respondent. The respondent filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate Authority which allowed the same on the ground that the appellant was in possession of 112 Bighas only and not 129 Bighas and 3 Biswas as held by the lower courts. In a revision application preferred by the respondent, the Board of Revenue set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer on the grounds that the petitioner was in posses sion of 112 bighas only and that he was in pos session of 112. Bighas even though he was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divi sional Officer on 5th May, 1976. The Board went on to hold that there is no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 and dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. In the writ petition filed before the High Court, the respondent contended that no appeal having been filed by him against the order, the said order became final and the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the sub Divisional Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the section confers executive powers of superintendence and control on the Board and it does not vest any power of superintendence on the board on judicial side. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 221 of the Indian Act is not subject to the other provisions of the , but is subject to appeal or revision. [726C] 1.2 The Board noticed that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order passed by the sub divisional Officer and consequently set aside his order of dismissal. The sub division Bench in the writ peti tion No. 681/79 dated 19th July, 1979 held that section 221 of 1955 is not applicable to judicial proceedings. [626D] 1:3 There was no provision in the Act for separate unit in Chapter 111 B of tho Act of1955 and the applicant Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional Offi cer, Hanumanthapuram, for fresh determination of the question of calling area for Raghubir Singh. The Revenue Appellate authority set aside this order on the basis that the respondent was in possess ing possession of the land of 112, Bighas. [ 728E F] 1 :4 In the instant case, the sub Division Bench held that there has been no provision of separate unit and dismissed it. [826C D] 2.1 The Board had by its order dated 14th April 1975 directed that the ceiling, area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1956 and it spite of it the Sub divisional officer committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Board. [750D] 2:2 There is no restriction on the powers of the board to set at naught the judicial orders of the courts. The Boards noticed that the Board has appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of supervision and control and the order was passed by them in appropriate cases. [751E F; 749A] 2 :3 There is nothing illegal on the language of section 221(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1955 to justify exercise of such powers. The board noticed that it has power in appropriate case to interfere with the judicial order of courts.

The first respondent, a journalist, was employed as an advocate in the newspaper establishments. The first respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur, calling upon it to implement the orders of the Central Government made under section 12 of the Act. The High Court accepted the plea of the first respondent and declared that the law reports published in the newspapers were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the . In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the Law reports published by the first Respondent are not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the Central Govern ment on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal is unsustainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by a first respondent are reports of recent decisions of the highest court of the land. Similarly, the decisions of every High Court being judicial precedents are binding on all courts situated in the territory over which the High Courts exercises jurisdiction. [785B] 2.1 In the instant case, the law report published by it is not sufficient to hold that the laws reports do not carry any news and that the public was not interested in them. The fact that a law report could be used as a reference book at later stage was not sufficient compliance with the requirement of section 12(b). [786C D] 2:2 In the present case, there is no dispute that the first respond ents published the reports of the First Respondent containing the decision of the High court. The First respondent, All India Reporter Limited and other publishers of law reports in the interests of their own business vie ws. [783F G] 2 :3 There is no doubt that the decisions contained information about recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. The decision contained in the law Reports may cease to be items of news after some time but when they are received by the subscribers they do possess the character of works containing news.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises. He continued to occupy the premises for five years and thereafter filed ejectment proceedings against him under section 41(1)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The appellant contended that he was a licensee and not a sub tenant. The trial court decreed the ejectment petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove that he had been a subtenant of the respondent and that the Court of Small Causes had no jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was a tenant of a monthly tenancy and therefore it was recorded that as agreed by the parties, the leave and licence agreement between the parties was renewed. The High Court also held that in view of the legal position and also the fact that the rent light bill stood in the name of the appellant showed that there was no desire to create any lease by the document mentioned therein and the appellant regarded him as a mere licensee. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to get the advantage of section 15A of the Act, the occupant must be in occupation by permission of the grantor that after the recovery of the permission a suit for possession could have been instituted under section41(1) of Bombay Rent and licence Agreement which expired on 31st March 1966. [1065B] 1.2 In order that an agreement creates a lease rather than a licence, it is necessary to obtain the licence from the grantor who has a subsisting agreement on the date of its filing. It may be that the non obstante clause of section15A(1), give him the status and protection of a tenant in spite of there being anything to the contrary in any other law or in contract. But if he was not a licensee under a subsisting agreements on the 1st of February, 1973 then he did not get the benefit of the amended provision of the Rent Act. [1165C D] 1:3. The question whether an agreement created between the appellant and the respondent is a lease and not licence depends upon the intention of the parties. It is well settled that in order to become a lease, it must depend on the intention or the contract between the landlord and the lessee. If he was such a licensee, the nonobstante clause of Section 15A(I) gives him the exclusive right to be put in possession of the property. [1266D E] 1 :4. The respondent had been carrying on business for some time and had produced rent receipt for the month of April 1971 for a monthly rent of Rs.56.25 p.m. inclusive of municipal taxes and had also produced light bill for the months of April, 1971 for the period 20.10.65 to 31.3.1988. The agreement recited that the licensee was to vacate the premises on 1st February 1973. The tenant was to be paid rent at the rate of Rs,56.50 p. m. inclusive. The landlord was also to pay a monthly licence fee of Rs., 56.25p.m., inclusive of Municipal taxes and a sum of Rs .2,500 for the year 1971. The licensee was not entitled to terminate the tenancy earlier than one month 's notice. The suit filed by the respondent against the appellant was dismissed by the trial court. The appellate court also affirmed the decision of the trial Court that the payment to be made to the respondent for the use and occupation of the premises was compensation and not rent. The Appellate Court upheld the finding of the Trial Court that it was a licence and not license. In appeal, this Court held: 1:5. The expression "licence" is used in section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, but the character of the transaction turns on the operative intent of the par ties. To put precisely if an interest in immovable property entitling the transferee to enjoyment was created, it was the legal result. [1366D F] 1.(a) The respondent was not the owner of the building and also denied that he ever had gone to occupy it. He was therefore a licensee. [1466E] (b) The appellant was not in occupation of any part of the demised premises and was not, therefore, entitled to protection under section 15(4A). [1467F] (c) The document in question did not create any tenancy by the said document.

The respondent was a Ruler of the former Dholpur State. He was assessed to excise duty under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that he had been assessed to income tax for the year 1947 48 and 1949 49. The respondent contended that the Ruler had no authority to levy any tax on the income tax as it emerged from the Covenanting State which came into existence after August 15, 1947, and that the United State of Rajasthan was a new sovereign and was not bound by any obligation imposed upon him by the new sovereign. Held, that the definition of "Government of the United States" in article 295(2) of the Constitution is wide enough to include the Government of the corresponding Indian State as it was on January 26, 1950 or would also include all the former States which came to be merged into it through the process to which the new State had been formed. The new sovereign throughout the territory of India, therefore, became a sovereign and could not be said to have intended to respect all the rights flowing from laws so continued and assumed all liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs Union of India ; , followed. Held further, that in view of article 295 (2) Of the Constitution the new Government had no right to levy tax on income as against the Ruler of former Jodhpur State in view Of article 295 of the Covenant which provided for the continuance of the old laws till they were repealed or altered by the New State. The United States of Rajasthan vs Jaipur State, ; , referred to. Held also that the new state was a sovereign State and was governed by the United Provinces of Rajasthan Act, 1947. The State of Ajmer vs Jaipur Rly. Ltd., [1959] S.C.R. 869, followed. Per Sarkar, J. The New State of Jaipur continued all the old law till they came into force and under the circumstances the new States became liable to pay tax on their income. The Act was a complete code in itself and could be applied to the Mills as it existed before the new Act came into operation. The newly created rights of the subjects of the merged State were to continue till they are repealed or modified by the old State. That is, the basic difference between the Dalmia Dadri cement Company case and the present case was that the old States had been merged in the United state of Rajasthan as a result of the merger of the erstwhile State of Jodhpur with the new Union. The rights arising under the old agreements were to be determined on the basis of the existing laws and the liabilities arising there under or even otherwise, provided the law so made was within the competence of the new 'State.

The appellant was a dealer in the sale and groundnut to the State Government. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, directing the constitution of a market committee at Virudhunagar, for the purchase and sale of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The appellant challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that they infringed articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions Of section 5 of the impugned Act were not violative of article 19(i)(f). The object of the legislation was to protect the producers of crops, particularly commercial crops, from exploitation by them and to secure better living conditions in the country. The Act did not provide for any restriction on the right to do business unless it was clearly established that the provision was too drastic and unreasonable so as to defeat the very purpose of the law. The provisions of section 5 were not only reasonable restrictions but also tend to defeat its object. The impugned provisions did not contravene article 19 (i)(g) or (g). The Act was an integrated one, and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crop and the bulk of transactions in such markets are regulated by the provisions contained in the Act. The fact that the growers may be under some difficulties in this regard does not affect the validity or otherwise of the scheme of the statute. The object is to protect them from being exploited by unscrupulous traders, who do business in the market established and run by them. The growing of commodities for money, the business of buying and sale and the purchase of goods at fair prices are regulated and controlled by the rules made under the Act and no restrictions on the fundamental rights of the petitioners can be justified as they are not prohibited from holding their property as property. The levy of sales tax is not a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 of the , but only an allowable deduction under that section. The contention that the appellants in C. No. 169 of 1955 were running the market as an occupation or business with high standards and that they were not prevented from doing their business for they could still be utilised for commodities other than those specified in the explanation is without substance. The definition of "trade" in section 2(f) of the Indian , includes trade allowance, which has been defined to mean a charge levied at a fixed rate for goods or goods specified in a notified area for the purpose of carrying on the business established by the Market Committee. The appellants were running a market as a dealer and were selling commodities at proper rates. The notification directing the establishment of a Market Committee for the sale of such commercial crops was not invalid because it had no reasonable relation to the object which the legislature sought to achieve. The exemption granted under section 5 was not only a trade allowances but also an allowable allowance under the bye law.

The appellant was convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the sentence of death but reduced it to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The conviction must be set aside as it is not based on any specific charge or evidence. It must be shown that there were no previous meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan. [1090 B] (ii)The appellant had been convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death, but the High Court was not satisfied with his conviction. His act fell under section 326 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The sentence of imprisonment for life would suffice. [1191 C D] (iii)The evidence showed that there was no previous meetings of minds between the appellant and the deceased and that they were not present at the time of the occurrence. There was nothing to show that the appellant had ever participated in the attack. It is only when the prosecution could prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted of the murder. [1102 C D]. (iv)The conviction under section 307 Indian Penal code must be reduced to transportation in these two cases mainly because of the difference of opinion between the High Courts and the Sessions Judges. The fact that the deceased had been attacked by the appellant did not warrant an inference of common intention in this case. [111 F G] (v)It is well settled that a common intention presupposes prior concert. In a case like that, each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that the separate blow with an axe was a serious one, it must be held to have been proved by evidence. [112 F G]. (vi)The sentence should be reduced from death to transportation. The appellant had not been convicted for an offence under section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal. He could not be convicted under that section for the murder which he was charged with. [114 B] In the present case, the appellant was guilty of murder and the act fell within the second part of section 326. [115 E F]. (vii)The High Court erred in holding that the death sentence should have been reduced to life imprisonment unless two Judges concur because of section 377 of the code of Criminal procedure. The appeal must accordingly be allowed.

The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order before the High Court on the ground that he was an officiating Sub Inspector in Class II service and was compulsorily retire by exercising the power under Rule 57(j) of the Fundamental Rules, as he had not at all been retired from service on 5.10.1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was an officer who was in Class I or Class II Service or post even when he held a permanent post and therefore, on the date of order he had completed the age of 54 years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that as the petitioner had not attained the age Of 55 years by the date he had attained the maximum age of 50 years, he could have retired from serv ice with effect on 5th November 1976 and therefore he could not be compulsorily retired under Rule 58(j). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of compulsory retirement made against each of the petitioners was set aside by this Court. [637C] 2.1 The requirement of officiating service in sub clause (i) is that if he is in Class 11 or Class III service or post, he has entered into service before attaining the ageof 35 years after the said servant attained the 55 years. He has entered service before reaching the age oF 50 years. [ 634D] 2:2 The requirement for sub clause(i) was not satisfied if he was in class I or class II service or Post, but on an officiating basis only. [337E F] 2 :3 The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) has a purpose behind it. If the condi tions indicated in sub cl.(i) are satisfied, namely, the Government servant is in class l or II service, or post and he had entered into serv ice before attaining that age of 35 years, and has attained the prescribed age of fifty, the further condition that he must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts cannot be introduced into the scheme. The object of Fundamental rules 56(1) is not relevant for determining whether a Government servant officiating in Class 1 or Class I service or a post even though he held an officiating appointment. [625E F; 626A B] 2.(i). In the instant case, the petitioner would have superannuated from service and, therefore, he cannot be resorted in service. He would have retired on the basis of the age prescribed by clause (1) of sub cl. (i). [626C D] (ii).

The respondents, who were the husband of respondent No. 1 and father of respondent Nos. 2 to 5, filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on the ground that the medical examination report was not submitted by the doctor in charge of the deceased and that the deceased had fulfilled his part of the insurance contract and the appellant corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards premium payable by the deceased. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondents were entitled to claim the amount along with interest at six per cent per annum from the date of refusal of payment till the date on which the demand was made and that it was not necessary for them to have any cause of action. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was a concluded contract between the deceased 's husband and the Corporation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf the appellant. On the other hand, there was an express provision in the Financial Powers Act, 1960 dealing with the financial powers. Indeed there was nothing in the Act which would justify a conclusion of the High court that there is a concluded agreement. The expression "underwrite" signifies acceptance by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [359E F] In the instant case, the appellant had not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case the Assistant Divisional Manager, to exercise the power of Divisional Manager. The Trial Court was therefore right in holding the appellant guilty of the charge and that he should have been acquitted. [360F G] 2.1 In view of the fact that such a long time has elapsed and further in view of finding that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal, the plea of Divisional manager being a mere formality is accepted. Acceptance must be signified by some acts or acts con cerned on by parties or through their agents from which it is possible and communicates his acceptance to the person making the offer. Whether the final acceptance is that of the assured or insurers, however, depends simply on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have progressed. [361H; 362A B] 2:2 In view Of the fact, such a short time has been elapsed and also further in the view that principal amount together with interest amounting to about Rs.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V. L. R. 60 IA. 76. The trial court granted an interim order restraining the bank from taking proceedings in pursuance thereof and directed the Bank to take any steps to take steps in execution of the decree. In appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and remanded the suit for trial. On remand, the trial Court passed a decree against the appellants. The High Court held that an order granting interim injunction was a final order as far as this Court is concerned and that the finality of that order was not to be judged by co relating it with the controversy in the suit. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) An order passed by the High court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding and leave the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the civil proceedings from which appeal has arisen is not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). The order refusing to grant an interim relief did not determine the rights of the party in relation to the matter in dispute in the court. [707 D E] (2) The expression "final order" in section 205 Cr. P.C., means a final decision on the rights or liabilities of the par ties, and that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights, and liabilities of parties is not a final adjudication on the right of the court, and therefore, an interlocutory order passed in such proceedings cannot be deemed final for the purposes of article 136(1) (a). [708 D E; 704 A B] Ramchand Manjimal vs Goverdhandas Vishindas Ratan Chand, ; , followed. (3) The order declining to grant interim injunction did not decide the rights as between the parties in the suits or proceedings and leave them to be determined by the court in the ordinary way. [700 G H] (4) The High Courts were right in holding that an application for a temporary injunction was not finally disposed of by the trial judge, and remanded it to him.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of cotton fabrics, was manufacturing cloth in the hands of the processor. The process of manufacture was done by the assessee and the process of manufac turing was done through job work. The assessee claimed that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth in his hands and not the value at which he would get the fabrics manufactured in the market, that the valuation should be adopted on the basis of the price at which the said manufacturer would be selling the processed goods in the factory gate for the processing on job work basis. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had paid the processor 's expenses and not to the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Assistant Collector. In further appeal before this Court it was contended by the Revenue that the transaction was a sale of processed fabric and not asessable price at the factory rate for the processed fabrics. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessable value is the value determined on the price of the grey cloth plus the value thereof. [345E] 2.1 The assessable valuation of the processing would be that the value would be Rs.30, being the value as at which it was selling the goods must be the price in which the assessee would be manufacturing the processed product and the person so authorised agree to discharge all the liabili ty under the Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at where the assessee is manufactured by another person are manufactured by a information is required relating to the price, plus the manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor in the assessable market which will either be included in the price as at the time of the manufacture or deemed to be the prices at the Factory gate for tho processed fabric. [346F G] 2:2 The assessablevalue of the process would be, the value, of the deter mination should be determined on a basis of price at that stage of the case. If the trader who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on the job work is required to discharge the duty under the said Act and rules made therein, it would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable valuation. [347G H] 2 :3 The assessable price at what he would be purchasing the processed cloth in terms of the job worked out is Rs.20 and the selling profit and expenses for the process are added to the value which will be taken for the price factory gate or deemed turing profits and the manufactured profit and manufacturing expenses, but not the other subsequent profits or expenses, and not any additional costs.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975, he was again promoted as Head Clerk. The Punjab Government notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Government. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that by reason of section 14(4) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973, the appellant could not be appointed as Head clerk in any event. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appel lant to the post of a Head Clerks prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be promoted as an Assistant or a Head clerk. He is appointed lawfully to the posts of a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [738C D] 2. The appellant was promoted on ad hoc appointment prior to June 13 1975, or the further fact that he was appointed in an ad hoe basis in January 1974, or, the further facts that he had been appointed as head clerk on April 1.1975, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13,1973 when the amending Act came to force. [750D E] 3. The fact that the appell lant was promoted to the higher post prior to December 1974 or the additional fact that him was appointed lawfully lo the post on April1, 1975 cannot improve the position for simple reason. Even if it had been made after May 13, 1975 when the amendment Act came in force, there is no justification for appointing him as a Sub Clerk since he was given promotion as a senior clerk on an Ad hoc basis in February 1974 or April 1975 on a regular basis.

The appellants, who were the disciple of a Math Sauna and were the Mahant, filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Saunti. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saana. On appeal by the plaintiffs, the High Court allowed both the appeals and held that the Amauli properties had been purchased by the Math, and that the income from the properties belonged to Math or the deity. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclea and must therefore be regarded as property belonging to the math or the temple of the Mahant. HELD: (i) The fund from which the Ama corpus properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. On his death in 1917, all those properties and wealth devolved on him from his predecessor Shivs Shankar Yati and he was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Ghazipur in respect of the two fixed deposits made by Mahant Shiv Sher Yati in the Bank of Bengal. Mahant Shiv shankar Yat is not a mere fact that a Mohunt is an ascetic does not raise any presumption that a property in his possession is not his personal property. [663 H] (ii) The income from properties belonging to Math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan, deepdan, daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. [665 B C] Gurcharan Prasad vs Krishnanand, ; , referred to. (iii) In assessing the income tax for the year 1950 51, the Amaulty properties constituted the Hindu Undivided Family of dedicated properties. The fund was constituted the Personal property of the appellant. On the death of Mahant, Shivshanker Yati, who in 1921 employed it for the purchase of the Amari and the Amarajanai Sanyasi, executed a will in 1956 bequeathing certain properties to the deity with the intent that arrangements for bhog were made for bhoga, deep faith and other expenses be met from them. The appellant was granted the succession certificate on the basis of the trust deed. The High Court was right in holding that the fund from where the Amaimari properties were purchased constituted the income of the Math and a claim to exemption from the levy was made.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were allotted certain quasi permanent allotments of land in the village of Raikot. The appellants challenged the allotment on the ground that they had been wrongly allotted to them under section 16(1) of the , and that consequently their allotment had been rightly cancelled. Held, that the Custodian was competent to cancel the allotment of land made by the appellants in favour of the appellants. The provisions of section 19(1)(a) and (b) of Act 1 of 1954 were applicable to a proceeding before an authority created by the . The power conferred on the Central Government under section 19 of the Act is not confined only to properties which are entrusted to them for management and not with respect to any other property. The Custodian, by reason of the divesting of the property, as from March 24, 1955 had become functus officio with respect thereto and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation of allotment. Bal Mukund vs State of Punjab, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. Held further, that section 10 of the 1954 Act does not help the appellants because there is nothing to show that a managing officer was appointed with respect of evacuee property or that he had acted in excess of his powers under section 17 of the . It is true that the provisions of sections 12 and 19 of 1954 are subject to rules made under the Act. But, as the appellants had been in possession at the critical time they would have had the right to obtain a permanent transfer in their favour of their property and by virtue of what happened and without any fault on their part they have been deprived of that right. The fact that the acquired properties had ceased to be evacuee properties does not make any difference because, as in the present case, the acquisition was for the benefit of the appellant 's family and it could not be said that section 19 (1) Of the 1954 was completely in conflict with section 10. The acquisition of property by the appellant was therefore illegal and invalid. Held also, further,that the provisions Of section 19 are subject only to rules framed under the Land Acquisition Act and not to any provision of the Land Acquisi tion Act. The contention that there is no entrustment in fact of this property or this class of properties to a managing officers or managing corporation cannot be accepted.

The State Public Service Commission issued a notification inviting applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Care ments) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Dulaji ousalodian of Girls schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (earch) District Inspecto rised by the State Government on May 5, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, a corrigendum was published on June 8, 1985, which was published in the newspapers and was published again on June 9, 1985 and was also published on the same day. The selection process was completed in two stage written and interviews/personals test. The appellant State Public Services Commission rejected the claim of the appellants for re holding the recruitment examination. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tions. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. [125B C] 1.2 The State Public Serv ices Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not be suffered. Public interest has been appropriately considered by setting down the four year in the instant case. [126C D] 2.1 The State Government should have be more careful to set aside the recruitments and asking the for a new interview of the entire recruitment examination and ask for a further chance to re hold of it. [127D E] 2:2 In lieu thereof, the State Public service Commission should also have been less careful in considering the matter. The situation could not have be deter mined by setting up the four years of recruitment test. [128F G] 2 :3 When no tice was pointed to set out in the advertisement and the advertisement rules fresh selections shall stand vacated.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of possession of the Dera and properties attached to it. The prayer in the plaint was that the appellant be declared an independent Dera as his successor in charge of the Shiromani Dera at Patiala. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, the respondent ceased to be the Mahant of the dera and the appeal could be continued under Q. 22, r. 10 of the Civil Procedure Code against the person upon whom the interest had devolved. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was filed on the basis that the appel lant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the respondent and that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be his mahant of the property. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 of Civil Procedure. [490 B C] 2. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest or for any other reason. Order 22 rule 10 is not confined to devolution of interest of a party by death, it also applies if the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such a case the successor to the head is sued under this rule. [489 C D] 3. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Dass was elected as mahant and that he was elected to be Mahant of Dera, could make no difference when the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [488 E F] 4. In the instant case, the suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant. The plaintiff was sued in his place and died during its pendency. Therefore, the appellant could not be added as parties under Order 22 Rule 10 of C.P.C. [ 489 F G] 5. The appeal must fail.

The Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board, which was a statutory body constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Act, 1948, framed regulations called the Hyderabad Civil Services Rules for the purpose of granting age of retirement to all Government employees other than in the last grade service. The Regulations were amended by the Andhra pradesh Electricity (Supply) Amendment Regulation No. 1 of 1979. By this amendment, the age of superannuation was raised from 55 to 58 years with effect from October 29, 1979 after an elaborate and scientific inquiry by a committee appointed by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The age of compulsory retirement was raised to 58 to 60 years with retrospective effect from November 3, 1977. The validity of the said Regulation was challenged before the High Court on the ground that it had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths who had already attained the age Of 55 years and that the age should be increased from 55 and 58 to 58. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amendment to the Fundamental Rules which introduced the age at 58 was not intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees and that even assuming that the regulation was retrospective, the decision of the Government was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the age. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The amendment made to the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply (Supply ) Amendment Regulation 1 of 1980 by which the proviso to rule 2 was deleted retrospectively from the date of the order in question in violation of the provisions of Chapters V and VI of the Constitution, is not valid. [658F] 2.1 The amendment to Fundamental Rules whereby the proviso was added to r. 2 was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature. By that amendment, a proviso was inserted to the effect that every Government employee, not being a workman and not belonging to the last Grade Service shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the age fixed by the lastday of the months in which the employee attains the last date of his month in the next following year. [600G H] 2:2 The amendment was made by the State Government in exercise of the power conferred by the proviso, to Article 309 read with article 313 of the Constitu tion. It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended as they can be made under the proviso. But until that is done, the exercise of power cannot be challenged as lacking in authority. There will be no order as to costs.

The appellants are dealers in raw materials in the State of Haryana. They purchased raw materials inside the State and exported those goods out of India. The respondent assessee purchased raw material inside the state from outside the State but paid no tax thereon, as they were registered dealers and furnished the declaration forms prescribed under section 24(1)(b) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessing authority assessed the appellant to sales tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of that Act. This claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that: (i) the words "in the course of export outside India" in section 5(1), are used in the context of sales falling under sub section (3) but not under sub s.(1) thereof, and (ii) the expression "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later on, clause (b) is used in relation to a sale or purchase within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "for the purpose of export" in sub s(1). are used with reference to sales and purchases that form part of his taxable turnover. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value of goods liable to tax under section 5 but the goods presently in question are not exigible to tax. [353B] 2. The expression "for sale" is defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in the course or export outside the territory of India within the term of sub s (1) and includes the taking out from the contract of sale entered into by the purchaser and would be one in the way of export. [354D] 3. The language of section 9 (1)(a)(i) later in point of time makes it clear contrast between sales fallingunder sub section(3) and those failing under sub sec tion (1). The words 'within the meaning ' are used to indicate that at least one of the three exempted categories mentioned therein is imposed on the sales and purchase. [355E] 4. The word 'export ' in sub section 2 (c) refers to goods which form part or parts of his assessable turnover. It does not include cases where the manufactured goods are disposed of only by way off sale falling under section S(3). [356F G] 5. The definition of "turnover" in s.2(c)(ii), however, is used with a view to include cases of despatches by a registered dealer for the purpose specified therein i.e. for the manufacture of goods specified in Schedule B. This term includes within its definition the purchase price of goods which are included in Schedule A. [356G] 6. The intention of the legislature was that the words 'for sale ' should be read ejusdem generis with the words used in cl. (a) and (b). The expression 'in the case of a registered dealers ' is defined to mean "the take out of, the goods specified therein" in the definition. [337B] 7. The Explanation to section 9 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1988 makes it abundantly clear that the word 'turnover" includes within it the taking Out of the taxable turnover under section 15. [359C D] 8. The explanation excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act". There can be no doubt that a tax is levied under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on them at the appropriate rate. [360E F] 9. The sale effected by the assessees falls within one of these two exempted categories set out in section 9. There can, therefore, be no levy of purchase tax under Section 9( 1) of Act.

The appellant firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The goods were sent to the sellers by the sellers on board the ship and they were delivered to the buyers on board. The sellers returned the goods to the seller on the ground that these sales were not their property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on the grounds that they remained the sellers ' property till they were brought on board and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). The appellant 's appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In further appeals to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the goods remained the seller 's property till after they had crossed customs barrier, and that therefore the exemption under article286(1) will come into operation. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b) are wide enough to include a registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The words " the time of the export" mean the time when the goods cross the customs frontier. The word " a registered dealers" is wide enough and includes a registered firm. In the United Motors case, the goods were on shipped by the seller and the contract was that payment will be made on the presentation of the bill of lading. The contract being that payment would be made at the time the goods reached the destination, the purchasing dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sold to a registered person. The fact remains that the intention declared has not been carried out. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 10 of the Act no purchase tax was leviable from them under article 285(1). The words 'a person " used in section 8(b), as a person ', were wide enough. The certificate issued by the Sales Tax Authorities did not show that the appellant had been carrying out the goods despatched by him or by a registereddealer to whom he sold the goods. The appellant could not be taxed under article 287(1), (b). Held further that the certificate of the Sales tax Officer was valid and the purchasing dealers were liable for having made a false declaration.

The respondent wife married the appellant 's second wife. She was a second wife and had a son by her. The first wife died in 1956. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. The respondent filed an application for maintenance under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 against the appellant and his father. The Magistrate found that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ . The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below had overlooked the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which provides that the woman has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was that there should be proof for maintenance. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 'S.127 rescue the respondent from his obligation. Payment of mehar money as a customary discharge is within the cognisance of that provision. But what was the amount of mehari ? Rs. 5000/ , interest from which could not keep the woman 's body and soul together for a day, even in that city where 40% of the population are reported to live on pavements, unless she was ready to sell her body and give up her soul. The husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 127(3) of Cr. P.C. [79 C D] 2. The expression "in which a marriage otherwise eligible, is entitled" in section 125 means a woman who has been divorcee by or had obtained a decree from her court and has neither claimed nor remarried". It does not mean that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The last defence based on mehar payment, merits more serious attention. [80 E F] 3. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available but here is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code. [81 G H] 4. If one were to locate a legal ground to raise the contention that the wife was not living separately by mutual consent, the court has spoken nothing to the contrary; and The High court has not spoken at all. Moreover, the husband has failed to prove his right to ignore the payment of the sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [82 C D].

The Collector of the district after perusal of the office note passed order on 25th March, 1988 under which he was directed to black list the appellant. The said order was challenged by the State Government in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the black listing of the appellant was not specifically mentioned in the order and that there was no requirement for giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the State that there is no requirement specifically of giving any notice under the rule of giving an opportunity to the appellant as he had been given a show cause notice and that the cancellation of the bid of the appel lant was not justified. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing order passed by the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation is concerned, that is not affected. This order will, however, not prevent the State Govt. or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for cancelling the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law. [868C D] 1.2 The order of the Collector dated 25th 3 1988 is set out in verbatim below: "Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Thakur, Village Repura, P.S. Puksha, District Samastipur has bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Singh S/O Late Gorakh Nath Village Repudwara, Pages. 1.3 The cancellation of bid of appellant is concerned. That is not effected. [886D E] 2. The order dated 25.3 1988 of the Collec tor is set quashed. So long as the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing the appellant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he was the landlord of the premises. The Rent Controller held that the building on the land leased to the respondent was not a vacant site and therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the rent controller 's order in respect of the said premises also could not be entertained. The appellant tenant filed an appeal against the order of eviction before the Rent Control Tribunal which held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1 had been only a vacant land, the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation of fair rent in respect thereof and that therefore the claim of the appellant was not barred by section 12(4) of the Act. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the Rent controller had no jurisdic tion to entertain an application for fixing fair rent under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease & Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948. On a reference made at the instance of the landlord, the High Court held that exhibit P1 was only a temporary piece of land and not a building site and that the claim by the appellant that he had decided to evict the respondent in the eviction petition under section 14(2)(vii) of Act was not correct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenant that since exhibit PI was a lease agreement, the rent Controller had jurisdiction to determine the fair rent and that, therefore, it was open to the Rent Authority to go into the question of title in view of the decision in the first set of proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that exhibit PWI was not open to challenge on the grounds of title. [562D] 2. Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Act is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent control ler by the terms of the Rent Act. It is an enabling provision which is available only for a vacant piece of lands and not of both land and buildings. The provisions of section 4 are intended to provide for a machinery for recovery of the amount. [563D] 3. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that where the Controller, on the language of section 5, has no jurisdiction in respect or other matters relating to the claim for arrears, he shall have power to entertain a suit by the defeated party and pass a decree for evic tion on any of the grounds mentioned in the said sections. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is not barred under section 12 (4) from examining a claim of title merely because the question may have had to be considered by the Rent Tribunal as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. [564D E] 4. Section 10(2) makes it clear beyond doubt that the Court of Small Causes is not competent to adjudicate on questions of title, and if the Civil court in this case had come to the conclusion that there was a relationship of landlord and tenant and that he has no title, yet, it would be open to him to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [565E F] 5. The question whether there is relationship of a landlord and a tenant and the land is not covered by section 10(1) or section 12, is only the determination as to the fair or standard rent of the land. If the Civil Courts in this respect are satisfied that there is a relationship between the parties, the landlord steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair and standard rent is and then fades out of the picture. Where a fair rent is fixed by a Controller, the Court has jurisdiction to adjudicate upon such matters as are not dealt with or ousted. [568F G] 6. The expression "any person" occurring in section 11(2), does not mean one of the direct issues before the Court.

The Mysore State Civil Service Integration Rules, 1960 provide for filing of objections against the preliminary provisional inter state seniority list. The appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to object to the final list. He filed an objection on behalf of Union of India that he was not heard after the final gradation list was prepared. The High Court held that the combined final gradation lists were provisional and directed the final lists to be prepared after hearing objections.
