In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant respondent was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the final select list was published. [828 D] Shankariah 's case, ; , followed. (2) The High Courts were under the misapprehension that the case now before them was also governed by what was held by this Court in Shankaria 's Case. [827 E F] (3) The principle recognised in Shankariah ' case was not applicable to such a case. [826 G] (4) The expression "initial or final seniority list" in Rule 115 of the Rules, which is an inclusive definition, means that certain principles are applied in the preparation of the list. These principles are generally found in the rules or executive directions which are known to or are capable of being found out by the persons affected. When a provisional seniority fist is prepared there is a possibility of some mistakes occurring about the facts of a case or in the application of those rules. It would, therefore, be quite fair to give a person affected an opportunity of making representations against the proposed final list, and the Central Government has also to give such full and fair opportu nity to the parties affected to make their representations. [825 G H] (5) The petitioner respondent was not given any opportunity to be heard on merits. [829 A B] (6) The petition is dismissed. [830 C D] (7) The judgment of the Mysore High Court is set aside and the writ petition is allowed. [ 831 E] (8) The Central Government, under section 115 of , has to determine the relative seniority of the parties in each case. If a final list is prepared according to the provisions of the Act, it shall be not finalised presumably because some mistakes had crept in due to want of hearing on two points.

The petitioners are partnership firm carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1988 was in force in 1985. In the year 1979 78, the import of raw diamonds was granted by the Export Houses, which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the Import & Exports (Control) Act, 1947. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant of Export House Certificate under the Import Policy 1978 79. The applications were rejected on the view that they had failed to diversify their export obligation as a condition for grant or renewal of licence in the Import and Export Policy 197879. The petitioner filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the rejection of the application. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the grant of Additional Licences under the Imports & Exports Control Act, 1985 is not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy, but also from importing articles which were specifically banned altogether as well as items which are banned for import by the holder of an Additional Licence; (ii) the Additional licences issued to Export Houses prior to April 1, 1988 cannot avail the flexibilities in import of items granted under the said clauses (ii), (iii) and (iv) of sub para (4) of Para 218 of the Policy 1978 80; (iii). The Additional Licences issued to the petitioners were valid for a period of 12 months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions; (iv). The grant of additional licences is to be determined on the basis of the export actually made in the three year base period 1975 76, 1976 77 and 1977 78. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The licences issued in favour of the appellants were valid only for 12 months, and the same period has lapsed during the period. Since the basis for the grant or the period of the Additional Licences which are entitled to this relaxation is different from the basis on which Additional Licences were granted to the appellants, the petitioners cannot claim the benefit of the same relaxation and assail the validity of sub Para 218(4) and also assail the legality of sub paras (10) and 215 of para 218 of Import & export Policy 1988 91. [244E F] 1.2 The licences in question are valid for the said periods of 12 month and the period has already expired during these years.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at the material time in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, and there fore, the goods were sold in bulk and delivered to customers at the appellant 's factory. The appellant had filed price lists in respect of the same. In respect of such consignments, the appellant was required to pay duty on the value of the drums manufactured by it. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise held that the goods are not returnable and hence the value could not be included in the assessable value. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the good were delivered from the factory in packed conditions and the packing was not returnable to the buyer; there fore the value had to be included as per the definition of "value" in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the order of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing contemplated in section 9(4) (d)(ii) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 for determining the "value", in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such packings" and not value. Therefore, it was held that where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of excisable goods, while determining the value, the cost of such packing would be includible in the value for assessment to excise duty. However, if any special secondary packing is provided by the assessee at the in stance of a wholesale buyer which is not generally provided as a normal feature of the wholesale trade, the costs of such special packing would not be includible. [995E F] 1.2 The cost incurred by the manufacturer and recovered by him from the purchaser whether as part of the sale price or separately, cannot be included under section 4 (4)(a) of Act. [996F G] 1:3. In construing section 4 of the Central Excises and Salt Act it is necessary to bear in mind that the measure of excise duty is price and not the value. The nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods arc sold at the factory gate is to be taken as the assessablevalue, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. The appellant was charged with having committed food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued his practice before the notice was issued to him. The prosecution case was that the appellant had taken food in a canteen for three days and he was demanding bribe of Rs. 100. On 21.10,1975, the appellant was alleged to have pressed the demand to PW 1. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and section 336 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appel lant was guilty. It is not a case that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant in his possession as a money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [357B] 2. The evidence of PW 1 is clearly incon sistent with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW l. This Court observed that though the conviction under section 165 I. P.C., and section 5 (1)(a) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I.p.c. The accused had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [340D] Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1, referred to. 3. In a case where the appellant started to take food there is no evidence that the money returned was the money return ed by PW I, the explanation offered by the accused was probable and there is nothing to show that the explanation arising under s 4(1) of Act is probable and probable.

The petitioner was an employee of a company which was in dire need of the flat in question. The Company had been in dire necessity of the premises and that the petitioner was given the flat for his residence during the period of his employment. The petitioner, however, continued to live in the flat till September 30, 1984 when he addressed a letter requesting the Company to permit him to continue to live with the flat as early as possible. It appears that the company refused to grant permission on the ground that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company 's rules. The company filed a complaint against the petitioner under section 630 of the Companies Act, 1971 in the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 37th Court, Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat and had instituted false and frivolous proceedings with ulterior object of protracting and delaying the eviction proceedings. The Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint against him and directed issue of process. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the petitioner holding that the view expressed by the Single Judge of the Bombay High Court in Amritlal Chum 's case was not correct and that there was no room for intendment. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the provision contained in section 630(1)(b) of the Act is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction; (ii) the words 'any such property ' in cl. (a) and (b) are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive; (iii) the legislature never intended to include past officers and employees of a Company within the ambit of section 630, and (iv) the expression 'any other property ' occurring in cls. (b), (c) and 545(1) of section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, is wide enough to include former or past officer or employee of the company; and (v) the Legislature never intended that a case where an officer or employees of the Company wrongfully obtains possession of any property of the respondent company during the course of his service was wrongfully obtained by an officer of a corporation, which was not entitled to be subjected to disciplinary action. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The words ' any such property" in cl.(a) are separable and independent. The expression 'other property ' is separated by section 6(1). By clause (b)(i) of sub section (1) by clauses (a), (b). creation of two distinct offences by clauses, (a ) and (c), which arise under different sets of circumstances, and it would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl. The legislature never wanted to include the past officers or employees in cls.(a), and therefore, both clauses (b and (d) must be read together. [176G H; 176A] 2. The word 'employee ' is used in the sense of a term of the profession which is characteristic of the draughtsman of the community. It is used to denote the existence of officers and employee or employees, and not to include others. The definition of 'officer ' in section 6 (1)(a) is wide and includes former or future officer or servant of the corporation. [177D E] 3. The phrase 'any person ' in clause (a). and (e) are separate or direct. The term 'or ` past officer ' means a present officers or employee who can secure possession of property of a bank during his employment, wrongfully withholds it after the termination of his employ ment. [179F] 4. The Legislature never wanted the word to include future officers and servants in cl (a); and therefore the words "any such officer" occurring in el. (e), are separated from the word "or" and therefore were clearly disjunctive. [180A B] Amritlal Chhum ' s case, referred to. 5. The language of section 629(1), which makes the wrongful withholding of property by a company, must be construed as including the words any such past officer etc.

The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was formed by the Maharaj who had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the said Sansthan. In the year of account 18,164 61 were purchased from the temple by one Vithal Rukhamai. The appellant 's father died in 1952. The widow of the Sansthan filed a suit for declaration that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The trial court held that the deity was a private property and not a private trust. On appeal the District Judge reversed the decision holding that the appellant was a public Trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and restored the order of the Charity Commissioner. The High Court in revision set aside the order passed by the District judge and held that it was a Public Trust under section 29 of the , and therefore the appellant 'was not a trustee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande. [523 B] (2) The expression "public trust" is a very important piece of evidence to show that a public temple is a private one. The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual as private property. [525 C D] (3) The definition of public trust contained in section 2 (13) and section 2 1(14) respectively of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, shows that the property has always been treated as trust property even by the Officer saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The definition is very wide in its application to a public charitable trust. [500 D E] (4) In view of the fact that the temple was dedicated for the Darshan by the appellant, the endowment was a religious endowment within the scope of section 29 and the High Court was right in holding that it had no appearance of any impediment or restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the public extending over a long period. [511 C D; 512 A] (5) The position and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property had been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property was dealt with, or managed, by those who were entitled to worship at the shrine of the temple, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a public religious endowment. [506 B C] (6) The fact that a person has been appointed as manager of a temple does not make him a private or a body of persons interested. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public character without the least interference or restriction from the Temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the State of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the character of devolution being that of a religious trust. Therefore, in this case all the above tests are fulfilled. [605 C D]. (7) The conduct of the appellant in the instant case shows that he was appointed by the founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public.

The appellant was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Marketing, Bombay. The income tax authorities issued notices to the appellant for payment of the assessed amount of tax. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notices by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 was void under article 13(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 16 of the Act had no application because the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis and the object sought to be achieved by the Act. HELD: (i) The assessment proceedings were started and the certificate issued by the Income tax Officer to the Additional Collector of Bombay was valid. [903 D] (ii) Section 46(1) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, which authorises the Collectors in different States to adopt machinery for recovery of arrears of land revenue, is clearly violative of Article 14 of our Constitution. The procedure prescribed by section 13 has been devised by the States for their own purposes which are closely akin or similar to the purpose of the Union. [803 G H] (iii) The provisions of the State laws relating to the collection of arrears and the powers of seizure under the Act have to be read into section 46 (2). The procedure provided in section 13 is that the Collector, on receipt of the certificate from the Income Tax Officer, has to proceed to recover the certified amount as if it were an arrear of land Revenue. [883 A B] Bhikaji Narayan Dhakras vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , followed. (iv) The procedure under section 13(2), which prescribes that machinery are not incorporated in section 46, is inconsistent with article 14 and therefore, the provisions of section 16(2). [804 C D] Bhikji Narayan Dhakas vs The Collector of Malabar, Nagpur and Another, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 905, followed. Bhikaji N Dhakras ' case, referred to.

The respondents were the owners of a Port Trust, who were employed in the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents were paid wages at the time of the initial appointment and the same was fixed at Rs. 10,000/ per month. The Trustees of the Port Trust claimed that under a scheme of 12hour shift with 8 hours ' work, overtime should be at least 3 hours if not 4 hours in the case of an adult, 9 hours ' working day. The Tribunal held that the respondents were entitled to a 12 hours ' shift and rejected their claim for a fixed period of rest. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on any single day the number of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 13(2) (c) read with section 13 (3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest and give an impression of what was meant by the interval of time. The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal working day because the total number of work hours in a week cannot go beyond 48. The workers are entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours on any day. In a 12 hour shift, the nine hours of duty on anyday can be spread over 10 days and the extra hours will necessarily be hours of the rest. The provision of section 15(2)(c) of the Act does not itself fix the hours for rest but only fixes the hours in case of a adult, and it is wrong to contend that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest; and if there is difficulty in giving the intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day, it cannot be said that the interval for rest shall break up the hours. In such an event it is not possible to fix only one interval or to make the interval more than 9. The rule of "lasting time" is made applicable by the latter part of section 55 of the . The reason, perhaps, is that in some employments time for work depends on some extraneous factors and hours of leave. In other words, the period must always be included as a period of days of rest, provided the period is specified beforehand, and the workman is neither called upon to work nor expected to work.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the respondent Nagar Palika Ghaziabad. The accommodation was let out on June 25, 1976. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 13(1) (a) of the Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for ejectment of the appellant from the premises before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop was let only on June 26, 1976, the provisions of the Act would not apply to these proceedings in view of the fact that though the premises were let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1, 1976 the provisions under the Act were applicable to these premises. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the premises had been let out for the first time on June 30, 1976 and during the pendency of this matter the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection of the provisions contained in the Act. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that in view Of the language of section 2(2) Explanation 1 it could not be doubted that period of 10 years would commence from the date on which the first assessment was due and so far as this question is concerned, it was concluded by a decision of this Court in Vineet Kumar vs Mangal Sain Wadhera, [1985] 3 SCR 491. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that since in view the language used in clauses (2) and (3) of section 39 of the Rent Act the appellant was entitled to the benefit thereof. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The rights of parties will be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date of the suit, but in Vineet. Kumar 's case the tenant will not be given the advantage of the provision contained in section 20(2). [165F] 1.2 In view of this decision of the Supreme Court in Om Prakash Gupta vs Mangal Sharma, ; , the appellant is entitled to get the benefit of the provi sions contained in this Act because the appeal will be a continuation of the proceedings pending before the High Courts for eviction relating to buildings brought under regulation for the second time in any suit for eviction of a tenant from any building to which the old Act did not apply. [165G H] 1:3 The right of the parties will he determined on its basis on the principles contained in sub section (2). It is true that the appeal is the continuation of a suit and therefore it cannot be said that the present revision petition or the appeal either to the High court or the appellate authority arose out of suit which was pending on the day on which this Act came into force. [166H; 167A] 1I1 In the instant case, the suit itself was filed much after the coming into force of the new Act. The appellant tenant could not therefore be given a advantage of section 20 of the .

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, who were the tenants under the appellant, and the third was the thika tenant. The trial court held that the appellant had not been liable to ejectment in view of section 29 of the West Bengal Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as amended by the West Benabari Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, which came into force on February 28, 1949. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was not liable to eject the appellant under section 3 of the Act as he was a thika tenants within the meaning of the said Act as it was finally amended by an Act of 1953. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 29 of West Bengal Tenancy Act 1949, which is prospective only, provides that where a landlord wished to eject a thikka tenant after the date of commencement of the Ordinance or proceeding which might be before the commencement of any court or before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the Calcutta Thika Tenants ' Act, 1950 for the time being in force as the case may be, he had to consider whether any of the grounds specified in section 3 were available to him and if so, he did not have to file a suit but apply to the Controller for relief on the basis that the applicant was a Thiika tenant within the mean ing of the provisions of the Bengal Thiaka Tenancy Act. [179 D E] (ii) The High Courts had rightly held that sections 4 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the ground specified in s.3 in order to succeed. There being no provision for transfer of pending suits and appeals, the court hearing the appeal would have to pass a decree for ejectment even if the defendant was a Thika tenant after taking into account section 3. [180 E F] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bangalpur Municipality, ; , followed. (iii) The landlord had not established any of these grounds specified under s. 3 entitling him to eject his tenant. [181 G H] Maha Deolal vs AdministratorGeneral of WestBengal, ; and Mahadeholal Kanojodia vs Estate Officer, A.I.R. 1953 Cal. 829, approved. (iv) The provisions of section 4 and the Explanation to s.4 of the East Bengal Thik Tenancy Act are prospective only. It could not apply to a case where a decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date on which the proceedings were commenced. [182 B C] Mahadolal, Kanodia, vs Administrator Gener al of West Calcutta, ; followed.

The State Government appointed a Pay Commission to consider the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. The Committee recommended that the post of Bench Secretaries be upgraded and placed in the pay scale of Rs.500 1,000. The State Government accepted the recommendations and issued an order dated July 2, 1976 appointing the Pay Commission (Amendment) 1971 as well as the Third Pay Commission Report. The High Court also directed that all Benches Secretaries to be given the same pay scale which is being given to Superintendents of Secretariat Offices, should be paid at least on par with Section Officers. The appellant State Government in its appeal filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated June 2,1976 and the High court allowed the petition. In the appeal by special leave it was contended that the nature of duties and responsibility of the two posts cannot be said to be equal; that the creation of two grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretary Grade II is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution; that there was no valid reason to give higher pay scale only to ten officers, and that the High Courts have completely overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules framed by the Chief Justice for promotion to Bench Secretaries Grade I. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay for equal work is not expressly declared by our Constitution to be a fundamental right. [302E] 2. It is well known that there can be and there are different grades in a service, with varying qualification for entry into a particular grade, the higher grade often being a promotional avenue for officers of the lower grade. The higher qualifications for the higher post which may be either academic qualifications or experience based on length of service reasonably sustain the classification of the officers into two grades without reference to seniority. [304G] 3. It follows naturally that equal pay is a concomitant of Article 14 of the constitution. But it follows naturally, that equal pays for unequal work will be a negation of that right. And this principle applies equally in respect of other posts even on seniority cum merit or merit cum seniority. The differentiation so made in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. [305B] 4. It cannot be denied that the quality of work performed by persons of longer experience is superior than the work of newcomers. The distinction made in this case is a reasonable classification. To hold otherwise, it would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service.

The appellant companies were incorporated under the , in the erstwhile State of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent 1, a Government Company incorporated under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, was constituted under the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1961. The appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent 1 for the Korba and other facilities for the development of the Authority in consideration of the authority given to it by the State Government. Respondent I was also a member of the State Legislative Assembly. The respondent 1 filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the demand for property tax made by the appellant company on the ground that no tax was leviable on its property since the Company was owned wholly by the Government of India and that respondent 1 could not impose any tax on its properties since it had been owned wholly or partially by the government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant companies did not fall within the definition of 'taxes ' in section 2(a) of the Act, and that the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the said two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d). In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that respondent I could exercise only such powers as were conferred upon the Development Authority under the M.P. Nagar Teshil Adhiniyam, 1961 and that since the appellant Companies had not been registered under the Act the Company could not be subjected to tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Legislature has the competence to enact the impugned law. It is well settled that in the instant case, the State Legislature was primarily concerned with the development and regulation of declared industries and not with the ownership of industrial undertakings. [14G] 2. In order to 20 judge whether on that account the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act of 1973 it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area Development Authority is given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [15H; 16A] 3. The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 127 A of the M .P. Municipalities Act 1961. It was not a tax on land or building owned by the Union Government. The lands and building on which respondent 1 has imposed the tax were used for the purposes of and are covered by coal mines. [16D] 4. The provisions conferring power of taxation provided for in section 127A of the Municipal Corporation Act, 1922, are beyond the legislative competence of the state Legislature; that is, it is not correct to say that the property tax provided for under the impugned Act of 1974 is beyond the Legislative competence of State Legislature; and that tax has nothing to do with the Development of mines. The power conferred by section 127(d) of Act of 1976 is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69 (d). [16E F] 5. The Corporation of the respondent had no authority to pass a law on the subject and the State Legis lature itself had no competence to legislate. [17G H; 18A] 6. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi is not competent to pass any law by reason of Entry 23, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [18B] 7. The Act of 1953 does not contain any independent provision or machinery for exercising the power of tax. The Legislature has no competence under Entry 24, List III to legislate on the topic covered by Entry 23 of List II. [19C D] 8. The contention that the Corporation carried on an industry under the authority of the Central Government within the meaning of section 2 (a) is without force because the Act is primarily concerned in the development, and regulation and development of coal resources. [20E F; 21A] 9. The question whether a corporation carries on an activity under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 or the Munici pal Corporation Act is outside the purview of Entry 54, List I read with Entry 24 of List 11 cannot be decided by reason only of Entry 52, List 1. [21F G] 10. The Central Act was primarily dealing with development and control of industries and cannot be said to have any competence to make the impugned legislation. [22G H] Baijnath Kedia vs State of Bihar & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was granted a lease for a period exceeding one year in respect of certain slate quarries within his estate. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease and the Collector confirmed the lease. On appeal, the Board of Revenue refused to ratify the lease on the ground that it did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide him with a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Board of revenue declined to raitate the lease but granted a certificate under section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The question for determination was whether the termination of the appellant 's lease by the order dated December 27, 1955, was bad as it did neither give three month ' notice nor provided for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act. Held, that the Board had no power to terminate the lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules of 1949 and the Government could not cancel the lease merely because the appellant had a right to claim compensation only when his right was terminated by the Government under the second proviso to section 20 (1). A mining lease granted by a private person shall be subject to certain conditions therein specified. The first proviso to r. 46(2) of 'the Rules provides that no such rights shall be enforceable against the Government unless it is created for a term not exceeding one month from the date of its issue. The second proviso also provides that the right created after July 1, 1945, was by force of the second Proviso and the appellant could terminate the tenancy with effect from the notified date. A mining lessee could terminate his lease only if he had been in the public interest that it should be terminated and that further, in such cases, compensation would be payable under section 21(2). The third proviso to rule 46(1), which provides for payment of compensation for the determination of rights created before July 1. 1945, provided that no right shall be enforced against the Govern ment unless it was created for any period exceeding two years. The third Proviso to r, 46(3) provided that a person can claim compensation under section 30(2); and the right conferred by the second sub rule could be exercised only if it was in the Public interest to do so and in such case compensation will be payable.
